subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the debate was adjourned yesterday I .was endeavouring by quoting figures to demonstrate the great mineral productivity of Northern Ontario, and I will ask the indulgence of the House to-day if I continue to quote figures in this connection, hoping that by so doing I may make known to the members of this House and to the people of Canada the wonderful wealth which we possess in northern Ontario. I feel, Sir, that we are on the eve of a tremendous development in that north country, and if by making known the wealth that exists there we can attract the attention of the youth of the land I have hopes that we may be able to check the exodus to the United States, for I feel that no part of Canada offers greater inducements to the young people of our country than the great northland.
The northland is comparatively new. The first discovery of silver was made in 1903. I have often heard it stated that the Temis-kaming and Northern Ontario Railway was constructed because of the discovery of minerals in the north. Sir, I wish to correct that impression. The Temiskaming and Northern Ontario Railway was built by the Ross government as a colonization railway, and it was during its construction that the first discovery of silver was made close to the town of Cobalt. Since that discovery, which attracted the attention of mining men everywhere, the area has been greatly enlarged. The prospector moving from the silver country gradually extended his operations until, a few years after the discovery of silver, gold was discovered at Kirkland Lake. To-day the gold camp of Kirkland Lake and Porcupine is one of the most interesting in the world, and we now possess in that north country the second largest gold mine. The production of gold has been increasing very rapidly from year to year, and it is the opinion of geologists who have visited this area that northern Ontario will soon become the largest gold producing area in the world.

The Budget-Mr. Lcipierre
la order that you may fully grasp how great this development has been, I will give you the figures of the production of gold since 1968. In 1910, the first year in which gold was shipped from the northland, the production was valued at 868,488. In 1915 it was valued at 88,501,391; in 1920, at $20,668,692, and for the six months ended July 1, 1923, the value of the production was $8,643,162. This gives a total shipment of gold from 1908 to 1923 of $116,454,125. This has all been accomplished within the last twelve years, and this great development in the north has taken place without any government assistance. The development is comparatively new, and when we consider the financial situation of the country and our transportation problems, it is easy to realize what an important part the development of these mines in the north is going to play in overcoming our difficulties. The dividends paid by the Hollinger gold mine alone from 1910 to 1922 amounted to $19,632,000. In 1922 the Hollinger mine treated 1,400,000 tons of ore, of a value of 812,700,000, and paid in dividends $3,198,000. When we stop to consider how the development of these mines in the north affects the whole industry of the country, it will be seen that the time has arrived for the people of this country to realize what great assets these are, and to assist in developing these great natural resources.
But northern Ontario does not possess mines alone. It offers greater opportunities for agriculture to-day than any other section of this Dominion. The great clay belt lying parallel to the Grand Trunk Pacific is now being rapidly settled by a hardy class of settlers, who find a natural market for their products in the mines. There is no more fertile land in Canada than is found in this northland, and there is room for thousands of more settlers to go in there and take up agriculture.
We have also in northern Ontario an almost unlimited supply of pulpwood and timber. W"e are developing sufficient water power for the needs of our mines, our pulp mills, and other industries, and we have besides a hardy, hard-working and intelligent population. Many of them joined the first rush of adventurers after the first discovery of minerals in the north, and they are now assisting in developing that northland. The district of Nipissing to-day is supporting a prosperous population of over 50,000, and we hope to see during the coming summer the biggest rush since the discovery of the camp.
Besides assisting in the development of minerals in the north there is left still
another great task for this government, and that is to, assist in the development of the iron ore deposits of northern Ontario. Ontario possesses an unlimited supply of ore.
It is sometimes called low-grade ore, but we have deposits of siderite which should not be classed as low-grade ore. The only difficulty we have had with our ore is that it requires sintering; that is, it has to be roasted and the deleterious matter driven off, but once it has been sinterized the ore is fully as of high a quality as the ore produced by the high-grade mines of the United States. We have now arrived at the time when the government must take into consideration the importance of developing these iron deposits. The high-grade ore deposits of the United States are now within calculable distance of exhaustion. Those high-grade ore deposits are now controlled by the large steel corporations of the United States, and every year we find the amount available to Canadian refineries considerably reduced. It is a known fact that the large iron and steel corporations of the United States now have their agents here in Canada looking over our ore deposits, and it behooves the Canadian people to see that Canadians be given the first opportunity of securing control of these deposits. We have assisted agriculture, live stock, and industry generally in this country, and if the government will give the same assistance in this case that it has given to others we can easily create in Canada a steel industry which will contribute immensely to our further industrial development. During the last ten years up to March. 1923, Canada had imported from the United States iron ore to the extent of 10,231,451 tons. During the last fiscal year the amount brought in was 701,993 tons. The reason that iron ore deposits in Canada are now closed down is due alone to the difficulty that exists in sinterizing the ore. At the present moment the large American steel corporations, realizing that their high-grade ore deposits are rapidly approaching exhaustion have commenced to sinterize their low-grade ore, and it has been demonstrated to the satisfactior of those interested in the iron and steel business in this country that Canadian ores can to-day, with slight assistance from the government, be made suitable for the furnaces. Canada requires and will require in the future large quantities of iron and steel. Our 3,500 miles of railway and our shipbuilding plants require the manufactured ore for ships, locomotives, rails, cars and other machinery. Our five and a half million farmers

The Budget-Mr. Lapierre
and our mining mills require machinery, agricultural implements and tools. Canada cannot produce these goods until it develops both its iron mines and water powers, and I might state that on the Ottawa river, in northern Ontario and part of Quebec, we have to-day sufficient water power to attract iron reducing plants. With the iron ore and the water power there, there is no reason why Canada cannot develop a great and flourishing industry. We all know how valuable to a country the iron industry is. I think it is safe to say, Mr. Speaker, that the iron and steel industry is the key industry of the world to-day.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on the budget I do not wish to take up much time in discussing either protection or free trade from a theoretical point of view. A number of years ago I had a friend who was a professor of economics, and he made the statement that no one could teach economics without teaching free trade. However, I am not going to occupy any time in discussing the question

in fact it would be needless-nor, in speaking of a low or high tariff, to add anything to the eloquent, instructive and convincing address that was delivered here the other evening by the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster).
I shall devote the time at my disposal this afternoon to revuewing to some extent the conditions that exist at present in Canada, and I shall say a few words upon some of the difficulties that face us and the possible means for overcoming them. Since the fateful days of August, 1914, we have been living under entirely new conditions. Nations everywhere have been seeking for some way out of the difficulties which now confront them, trjdng to adjust themselves to the new conditions which have arisen, and to resume their normal course of progress. In almost all cases this has been found to be no easy task. Captain Sinclair, speaking the other day before the Canadian Club in the Chateau Laurier, made the statement that throughout the whole continent of Europe the material and economic conditions could be characterized as nothing but shreds and patches. He also made a further statement, that to me suggested cause for anxiety-that in a great portion of Europe to-day moral and religious feeflings have almost ceased to exist. I hope, Mr. Speaker, the latter statement is not true, because if religion and morals go all will go. I hope that the conditions in that respect at least are nothing like as bad as Captain Sinclair portrayed, after having made a tour of Europe 
which lasted almost three years. I think he also made the statement that in Italy the population was increasing rapidly and production decreasing-that there were more feet below the table and less food on the table. Now, that is the state of affairs we find at the present time; thirty-six nations trying to adjust themselves to new conditions, to new physical boundaries not always drawn in conformity with race, or religious belief, or even economic interests. What are these nations doing at the present time? We find them building up high tariff walls, making it more difficult to have a free interchange of commodities, keeping alive the passions, the hatreds and the jealousies that have worked so much evil in that old continent up to the present time. I think every student of history will admit that after wars have passed away, after the din and the tumult have died down, and people have the opportunity to consider just what the causes of those wars were, it has generally been found that they originated in desire for territorial aggrandizement or commercial expansion. I claim, Mr. Speaker, that the confusion in Europe to-day is greatly intensified by the fact that the nations there have not cultivated any friendly sentiments in the way of commercial intercourse or interchange of commodities; they have rather built up high tariff walls one against the other. We are getting no light or leading from the continent of Europe to-day.
Now, we are told continually that because other countries are adopting high tariffs we should do the same. But that is one example that I am not prepared to follow. When we come to Great Britain what conditions do we find there? Think of those wonderful islands, think of Great Britain the mother of nations, and her tremendous achievements! In these days I think we are very proud of the Old Land. With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I shall read a clipping that I took this morning from the Ottawa Journal. Doubtless most hon. members have read it, but nevertheless it is so good that I wish to place it on Hansard. The article is entitled "Hats Off to Britain." and reads as follows:
Britain's financing stands as a continuing marvel. Before the war there were those who saicf (some said it gleefully) that the people were decadent, that her financial, moral and physical foundations were crumbling, that she was going the way of the great empires of the past. Britain's answer was to fight the most colossal war in history, to pour out blood and treasure unstintedly, to buttress and finance most of her Allies, to write deeds of heroism, fortitude and courage that will live while men remember.
And since the war, what has been her record? While other nations bowed before the aftermath of the Btorm, she has marched from triumph to triumph. Her
MAY 1, 1924	[DOT]
The Budget-Mr. Forke
word her bond as of yore, this " Perfidious Albion " has fulfilled her every obligation. Reeling under a world-wide catastrophe, beset by troubles at home and abroad, dragged down by creditors who either would not or could not pay, she has paid her debts, paid to the last farthing, asked for no favours other than her due, and is emerging from the tempest with honour unsullied and her credit and name unimpaired.
.	.	. .And that credit is being maintained under
the leadership of Ramsay MacDonald. During the past year Britain faced prodigious problems at home and abroad. She encountered unemployment, strikes, and industrial depression. She paid out millions and tens of millions for pensions and doles. She had to maintain a mighty army and navy. And she had to face all the expenditure 'incidental to the administration of an empire which embraces one-fourth of the world's territory, and one-third of its population.
Yet this week she produced a surplus. Produced a surplus of $240,000,000: and in consequence, reduced her floating debt by $175,000,000; abolished her corporation tax; and lightened the food taxes of her people.
Yes, hats off to Britain! In peace as in war she stands as the spearhead of progress. While other peoples have let strife visit them with chaos, she has toiled for peace and reconstruction. In a world of turbulance and hatred she has not been afraid to disarm. And while racial suspicious and greeds and jealousies have been turning the world into a Witches' night, while parliamentary government has been going down all over the world, she has been giving a magnificent example of the robustness of her democracy, extending the boundaries of freedom in her Empire, and to-day, after 1,000 years, the greatness of her dominion knows no westering sun. To-day, indeed, we can say of her, in the words of a celebrated poet:
Set in this stormy northern sea,
Queen of these restless fields of tide,
Britain! what shall men say of thee,
Before whose feet the worlds divide?
I want to point out to the House Mr. Speaker that the nation depicted in these glowing terms is free trade Britain. Some hon. members to my right have stated that Great Britain was not a free trade country, that to some extent she is a protectionist land. In the main there is no doubt that the United Kingdom to-day is a free trade country.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They also stated that Great Britain was a nation of paupers. .

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I think I made the remark
yesterday that conditions in Great Britain were not really so bad as some hon. members seem to believe. I think the editorial which I have just read from a newspaper which is, perhaps, not friendly to free trade ideas, is well worth repeating. The other day I received a copy of a newspaper published in my old home county, in Scotland, sent to me by someone in Toronto whom I never saw. I read it very carefully, as I was interested in the different items of news from a social and business point of view. Trying to read between the lines in order to find out the social and business conditions existing in the 105
locality in which I was born in Scotland, and without prejudice trying to find out just what was being done over there, I could see no great indications of any - tremendous troubles in that country greater than we are experiencing at the present time. Social life seemed to be swinging along pretty much as usual, and, judging from the wage report, I could not see that there was any material difference between the agricultural workers in Scotland and those in Canada at the present time.
I turn now to the United States for a few minutes. The United States is held up to us as one of the great examples of what protection can do for a country, but I would like to point out that the United States has great advantages in climate and natural resources. Perhaps no country in the world has the same advantages as the United States in these respects. Coming to more recent years, the United States was enabled to realize huge profits from war contracts before she ever entered the war, and in no way can you compare protective United States with a country which has been in the same position as warworn and weary Europe is at the present time. I am going to speak more about the United States later. We have no reason to compare the condition of Canada with the condition of the United States. The burdens which are being carried by the United States, with its wealth and population, cannot be compared to the heavy burdens which Canada carries at the present time. Canada entered the war, made sacrifices in human life, money and wealth and in every way incomparably greater than any sacrifices the United States has made. Therefore United States' prosperity and Canada's trouble cannot be compared in any way, through either the tariff or the want of a tariff; that has nothing to do with the question in any shape or form. In Canada we have a rich and fine country with great natural resources. The hon. member who 4 p.m. has just addressed the House (Mr. Lapierre) dwelt upon the mineral wealth of Canada. I had the privilege to-day of listening to an address in the Chateau Laurier by Professor Wallace, of the University of Manitoba. He was at one time commissioner for northern Manitoba and I think also president of the Mining Engineers' Institute. He is a man well acquainted with the mineral possibilities of Canada, and it was cheering indeed to listen to the address in which he stated what he considered to be the possibilities of our future development in that .line. He spoke of that vast stretch of territory to the north which is sometimes the despair of some of us who wish to see Canada

The Budget-Mr. Forke

a united country. Speaking of our mineral wealth, he believed that mining and lumbering and other industries would bring about such vast development in that vast stretch of territory that it would link up what we now call the East and the ' West into one complete whole. Canada has a temperate climate.

speechtext: Would the hon. member tell the House what Professor Wallace said about industrial development in the prairie provinces?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about industrial projects?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I was going to come to that later on. if the hon. gentleman had waited. But I will say a few words, now that he has called my attention to it. Professor Wallace pointed out that the vast resources in the prairie provinces in the shape of coal would make it quite easy for that country to be. developed from an industrial point of view; and that in time to come industries would grow up upon the prairies, and, that we would have a more diversified production than we have at present. I am sure I do not wish anyone in this House to believe for one moment that I am not in favour of industrial development. I do not think any member in this House would have anything to say against industrial development in Canada. The only fault we have ever found is that an attempt has been made to foster some industries which seemed to be unable to suit themselves to the conditions found in Canada.
With reference to the budget brought down by the Acting Minister of Finance, (Mr. Robb) I am sorry that he is not in his place, because I would like to have complimented him upon the businesslike way and the intelligent form in which he presented that budget. But I have some little criticisms to offer. I think the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton), in that short speech he made after the budget had been delivered, stated -rather jauntily that it was a matter of bookkeeping whether you had a surplus or 
a deficit. Perhaps it is a matter of book-keeping, which is rather staggering to the ordinary man in the street, but I am sure that there must be something more than just book-keeping behind it. and there must, in a financial statement, be either a balancing of accounts, or a surplus or a deficit. I am not going to enter into any discussion or analysis of that financial statement. I think most of us have a complete grasp of it and know exactly what it means. To some extent at least it is very satisfactory from one point of view, namely, that we have at last turned the corner and are moving in the right direction, and that in the not far distant future some reductions will be made in our national debt. I agree with the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) that a financial statement might be made in such a way that all the commitments of the country and its liabilities could be stated so plainly that the ordinary man in the street would understand just exactly what the financial condition of the country was. I know that almost all finance ministers, Dominion and provincial, have a universal habit of making as favourable a statement as they possibly can. I have heard it said that this is done to help the credit of the country and to make the best showing possible, but really I do not think it can amount to very much after all, because when we are dealing with financial people, surely they are quite able to analyse a financial statement and will do so, and really it does not matter very much if in that statement, the very best showing is made, to help the country, I think that all the liabilities for which the country is accountable should be clearly understood by the people; they should not be charged at random to this account or the other, but should be so set out as to be intelligible to the ordinary man who sometimes is bewildered by our present methods and certainly does not know just where we stand.
Let me say a few words in regard to the necessity for economy. We have great national obligations, huge war debts, heavy fixed charges and liabilities in connection with our national railways, all of which must be met. Unfortunately, all governments, Dominion, provincial and municipal, have spent money rather too freely during the last decade, with the result that taxation has assumed considerable proportions. A great deal of the obligations for which the people of Canada are to-day responsible are fixed charges which will have to be met for several years, and we must realize to-day that for some considerable time yet to come the road before us will be a difficult one. This

The Budget-Mr. Forke
increases the necessity for the most rigid economy in the conduct of our public business, whether it be on the part of the Dominion government or the smallest municipal council. Any one who has had anything to do with public business knows that people in office always have demands made upon them which are larger than they can possibly undertake. That is common experience; certainly I know it is the fact in municipal affairs. I believe that society generally to-day is demanding greater services and more conveniences than it is willing to pay for, and that is one reason why people in office should be exceedingly careful about expenditures. I think it was Samuel Butler who said that progress first began when man sought to live beyond his income. On that principle it seems to me that we are progressing rapidly nowadays. I have no doubt there is a germ of truth in the suggestion; because if wTe are entirely satisfied wTith our conditions we are not likely to make much progress. At all events, I think that every one who has anything to do with the spending of public money should bear this truism in mind. There are, however, certain public services that should not be neglected, no matter what our views on economy may be. For example, whilfe the question of public health refers perhaps more particularly to the provincial sphere, I think it is one of the utmost importance. Under no conditions should anything appertaining to the health and the physical welfare of the people be neglected; that would be fclse economy, and I trust that both Dominion and provincial governments will carefully avoid it.
Another important department of public service is the education of our people. I know that a very long address might be delivered on the question of education, and I do not think there is a member in this House who would not have at least some views to contribute to a discussion of our system of education and its results. We no doubt all agree that it is one important phase of our national life that calls for the greatest attention, and	while	economy
should be practised to as great an extent as possible, nevertheless all needful expenditures in this direction must be made. Now, the term "education" is comprehensive, it is very wide in its application; and an important aspect of education is the training of men in engineering, mining and similar industries. Perhaps that is a side of the subject that we never think of, and I would impress upon the House that while our young people are being educated for the purpose 105i
of pursuing various lines of endeavour, the dignity of labour should always be upheld.
I think that ive are going astray a little in this respect. The man who soils his hands in honest labour to-day is not, I think, received with sufficient respect by the great bulk of society. I sometimes feel, as I have no doubt most people have felt, that .when one has done a creditable piece of work, either physical or mental, he has created something which in some way or other will be of service to mankind; and there is certainly a great deal of satisfaction to be derived from that source. I want to see labour dignified everywhere as something honourable, so long as it serves society and contributes to the general happiness of the people.
I want to say a few words about manufacturing, and I confess that I enter upon this ground with the greatest timidity. Of course, a number of hon. gentlemen in the House are accustomed to addressing us on this side on the subject of agriculture, telling us what we ought to do in order to carry on our business. So that I may presume to say something to the manufacturing interests, though I shall be rather cautious in what I say. I have no other wish than to see our manufacturing industries prosperous. In the past few weeks there have been many complaints regarding conditions in connection with these industries. I have received letters from almost every place where manufacturing is being carried on in Canada, indicating how dangerous and critical a position that particular industry occupies at the present time. In these communications I am told, virtually, that it would be criminal to do anything that might tend in any way to injure the business. Now, I am not inclined to take so gloomy a view of the thing, nor do I believe that the manufacturing interests themselves are as pessimistic as some of them pretend,-perhaps I should not use the word "pretend," but hon. members know what I mean. I have watched the agricultural implement people and I want to give them credit for this fact, that since the budget has come down I have not noticed very much *whining on their part; rather, they are buckling down to work, and the first thing we know, the agricultural implement industry will be prosperous in the next year. It has struck me as something rather strange to notice the general tone of the prospectuses that are put out by several manufacturing concerns to-day. The account that they give of themselves in these documents is very different from the one which they give when writing to some hon. members in this House.
The Budget-Mr. Forke

I have no doubt that members of the government get these letters, too. The prospectuses, I say, tell an altogether different story. For instance, I notice a prospectus issued by the Howard Smith Paper Company appearing on the first pages of MacLean's magazine, and the statement is a very bright one. They are selling their bonds guaranteed at 7 point something per cent and they say that they have cheap power, that they cannot supply the domestic demand, and that their export business is growing rapidly. One of the things that bother me a little-and I do not think that I am misinformed-is the fact that this company is selling its products cheaper in the United States than it is selling them to Canadian consumers. I suppose this would be called dumping. We hear a great deal about patriotism and the love of people for Canada, and we are urged to see that Canada shall prosper, and so forth. Yet those people who talk that way turn round and charge their fellow countrymen a higher price than they ask the foreigner to pay. I know very well everything is not flourishing; in the United States also manufacturing concerns are closing down through over-production. I put it another way-not over-production, but under-consumption, lack of demand, inability of the people to purchase the goods that are being produced. We had war industries and over-stimulation; to-day we have industries that are over-developed, over-capitalized, and consequently burdened with too heavy overhead expenses. These are our troubles.
How do some members want to remedy these evils? They would put the tariff up a little higher, in other words charge the people a little more for the goods that even at the present time they are unable to buy. Because, Mr. Speaker, there is no other conclusion to be reached: If you are going to raise the tariff it must be for the purpose of raising the price of the manufactured product. I claim that to-day the trouble is not over-production, but inability on the part of the people to purchase the goods that are being produced.
Now a word in regard to the employees of some of our industries. I know' very well what their feelings must be when they get slips in their pay envelopes such as we have received copies of. They are very human, they are people just like you and me. When they open their pay envelopes and find a slip to the effect that if a certain line of fiscal policy is followed the concern for which they are working will be closed down and consequently they will be out of employment,

w'e can easily imagine their feelings. They are going to be afraid of losing their jobs, and therefore when they have the opportunity they w'ill vote in favour of the policy which their employers tell them is the only policy by which the industry can be maintained. I think, Mr. Speaker, that this is a very unfair method to employ. No one presumably is prepared to deny the authenticity of these slips, some of which I have in my office upstairs.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen may laugh.
They may think that an honourable way of doing business; I do' not. It is the very cheapest kind of propaganda, for those engaged in it are not even paying advertising rates. We hear a great deal about maintaining the high standard of living of those engaged in Canadian industry. Of course, we are told that it can only be maintained by means of the tariff. The inference might be drawm that if you want to reduce the tariff, then, as a matter of course you wan' the workers in our factories to accept a lowe-standard of living. But in reality nothing is further from the fact. None of us want to sfee Canadian workmen forced to accept a lower standard of living. What are wages- real wages? What are the wages that the average working man or working women gets to-day? Briefly these wages represent food, clothing, shelter, some luxuries, a little play, and something to lay by for a rainy day; that is what I may call adequate wages for working people. Forty years ago I happened to live very near a large manufacturing centre in Scotland-Galashiels and Selkirk. To-day the people there are carrying on just as industriously as they ever did. It is a lone time to look back to, but my recollection of the people who were working in the large factories in that district at that time is this: The men and women were neatly dressed, and their standard of living forty years ago was just as good as the standard.' of living of our industrial population to-day. Such a statement may perhaps be questioned, but I think it is correct. I am inclined to believe that the standard of living of those employed in the free trade factories of England will compare favourably with the standard of similar w'orkers in any protected industry in Canada at the present time.
To-day a dollar buys less in Canada than in any other country. The cost of living is high, the cost of production is high, and consequently our manufacturers are not able to

The Budget-Mr. Forke
compete in the outside markets. In a word, we are working round in a vicious circle. I know it is quite natural for a man in receipt of high wages to complain if his wages are reduced. But if you increase the purchasing power of his lower wages he will be just as well off. High wages deceive working men, for certainly they do not add anything to his well-being if everything he has to buy is high in proportion. This, as I said before, is the vicious circle. It may work out apparently satisfactorily while one industry is able to charge another industry high prices, but when the primary industries have to sell their products in the markets of the world they find themselves at the bottom of the pyramid and in the worst state of any class in the Dominion.
We have heard a good deal from time to time in this House about a protective tariff compelling American industries to establish branch factories in Canada. Well, I saw a statement the other day-I hope it is not true-that the economic control of Canada is rapidly passing to Wall street.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, I hope it is not true.
But what are the facts? What are the American industries now located in Canada doing to develop this country? They are owned by American capitalists, and a good many of them are absorbing Canadian concerns. But over and above all, most of these American factories are simply nothing more nor less than assembling plants, established here to take advantage of our tariff. I do not think this is likely to develop our country to any very large extent. I saw a statement recently that 31 per cent of our Canadian industries are connected in some way or other with American capitalists. This perhaps may not be true, yet I think probably it is truer than most people will admit. This, it seems to me, may be termed peaceful penetration. So when we boast about our tariff policy compelling American concerns to establish branch factories upon Canadian territory, the effect may be such as we had never contemplated. I am inclined to believe that our national structure will be built on a much safer basis, on a low tariff basis, on almost a free trade basis, rather than on a high protective tariff resulting in the establishment of American branch factories on this side of the line. American concerns have been assembling in their Canadian plants parts of American-made automobiles for. export to Great Britain, thus securing the advantage of the British preference and putting money into their pockets.

Just a word in regard to our home market. We hear it remarked so often that the Progressive party have no use for the home market. I do not think anyone despises the home market. The home market is good, and we want all we can get of it. I would be only too happy if Canada could provide a home market for all its products at fairly reasonable prices, so that we might all live happily no matter what industry we are engaged in. But surely, surely, hon. members to my right who have been lauding the home market as the solution of our economic difficulties must realize that, measured by the progress we have been making under the National Policy, it will be generations before the home market can even begin to consume any large proportion of the products that are raised in this Dominion year by year. They have high protection in the United States, where there is a population of a hundred and ten millions. Hon, gentlemen tell us that the condition of the American farmer is a great deal worse than the condition of the Canadian farmer, yet in the same breath they say that if we had a larger and more diversified population the troubles of the farmer in this country would be over. The farmers in the United States are beginning to understand that when that country reduces her imports there is a condition which militates against the ^prosperity of the agricultural population. But, Mr. Speaker, I believe the day is not far distant when we are going to see a change of policy in that country from the one that is at present being followed. The United States has prospered not because of a high tariff policy, but in spite of a high tariff policy. They have a varied climate, they have great natural (resources, they have an immense area within which free trade prevails. Just imagine, if you can, the thirty-six nations of the old continent of Europe cutting down their tariff walls and following the example of the United States-because if they did that they would be doing no more than the United States is doing to-day. If that could be done we would have that old continent rejuvenated in a very short time; at least its condition would be a great deal better than it is now. The United States is no example of the benefits of a protective policy.
I want to say just a few words about the policy of the Progressive group in this House. I think I saw it stated in the Montreal Star the other day that the Progressive movement was more than a political movement and that there was a necessity for it from the economic point of view. The editorial went
The Budget-Mr. Forke

on to point out that the condition of agriculture, especially in the West, I think it said, was serious, indeed was almost tragic. I do not want to emphasize that any more than is necessary, but of course the Star had a different solution for these difficulties from that which the Progressives have been advocating in this House. At the same time I think it was a good deal for the Montreal Star to admit that we were not playing politics, that there was something more behind the Progressive organization than a political movement, that it was an economic necessity that brought the Progressives into the prominent part that they have been playing in the public life of this country. In fact, the Star admitted that there was good reason for their existence, that they came into existence because there was necessity for their being- I am paraphrasing the statement of the Star. I hope that we are not going to hear any more assertions to the effect that we are playing politics.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh. oh.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well I am very glad to be
able to afford my hon. friends to my right a little amusement. We have been the subject of a good deal of criticism from that quarter of the House during this session. It is the privilege and the opportunity of my hon. friends to do that, and if they are at all pleased to do it I am sure that hon. members on this side have no fault to find with it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The same with us.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The flowing tide is with this movement. We are confident in the belief that the development of the primary industries will under more favourable conditions make for the prosperity of all the people, and of the secondary industries as well. We want something that will be for the benefit of Canada, not for the benefit of any particular province. We hear a great deal about the policy that was inaugurated by Sir John A. Macdonald, but we are not living in the Canada of Sir John A. Macdonald to-day. Vast commercial and economic changes have taken place in Canada since those days. A great new factor, a huge producing and consuming power, has come into Canadian life. Twenty-five years ago the western prairie provinces had little effect upon the public life or the commercial life of this country. Let any member of this House honestly ask himself -what effect the crop prospects of western Canada have upon the whole Dominion at this time. Every year from springtime until the wheat begins to roll over the

railways to the markets of the world, every man in business, every man engaged in manufacturing is watching the crop barometer to see what its effect will be on the business life of the whole community. Does anyone say that conditions are the same to-day as they were in the days of Sir John. A. Macdonald? Are we forever to be tied up to traditions of that kind? Are we never to take any step forward? Is there to be no improvement? We have been passing through difficult times; we have been looking for help, for guidance, for a solution of our difficulties, and what are we getting from my hon. friends to my right? A little higher tariff; increase the cost of production, they say, and all your difficulties will vanish. I am well aware, that if you were to obliterate the tariff all our difficulties would not be solved, and I do not think any hon. gentleman in this part of the House will think differently. But we believe that a lowering of the tariff will help conditions materially for everyone concerned.
I repeat that there will be no real improvement until the cost of production has been lowered, and this is where industry can help. I do not believe that the condition of industry in Canada is so terribly bad as. we are led to imagine. I cannot help but think that we have Canadians with enough intelligence, enough natural ability, enough business sense, given proper conditions, to produce in Canada and to compete with any country in the world. Why can we not do it, if we get the raw material and the labour? We are continually told that 'labour is higher here than it is in other producing countries. Well, I have questioned that, because wages have to be gauged by their purchasing power and the purchasing power of wages in Canada to-day is not much better than it is in a great many other countries. Of course, we are always asked to look to that highly protected country on the other side of the line, where wages are just as high as they are in Canada, and we are told that we cannot compete with that country of high wages. Sometimes you hear about "mass production", but we can never ha ve mass production under the present circumstances. If you will allow me to make a personal remark Mr. Speaker: When I was home at Easter the young man I have in charge there said he would like to get a double disc drill. I have two very good shoe drills-farmers will understand what I am talking about, and probably the rest of the House will. But this man is young and quite ambitious and I thought I would like to please him. I went over to the town and asked what was the price of a double disc

The Budget-Mr. Forke
drill. The reply was, $266. Well, I just gasped.
I went home and I said "You had better cultivate ahead of the shoe drills and we will do without the double disc drills". That is exactly the position of the farmers on the prairies; they are unable to purchase the goods that are being produced. Will it help business if you add 10 per cent to the price of that drill and make it almost $300? Will it make industry flourish and prosper to produce another drill that nobody would be able to buy?
I want to be dear on this matter; I want to be fair and honest with my friends to my right, because I think if we could really understand each other, perhaps there would not be so much difference in this House as there seems to be sometimes. I speak more particularly with regard to our implement manufacturers to-day,; I think the trouble with the Massey-Harris Company, for instance, is not the cost of their production, but that they are not able to produce in sufficient quantities to make their business pay, in view of their overhead expense. I may be wrong, but that is my opinion, and we are not able to get that increased consumption until we get prices lowered, and I have been trying to show how we may be able to reduce prices.
I admit that in rehabilitating this country agriculture has to do its part. I am not going to tell industry and business that they have to do so and so and that agriculture can lie down and accept conditions as they are, even in carrying on its own business. Changed conditions require changed methods, but no artificial bolstering of weaklings will help business or the farmer. There must be business methods and industrious habits. I am not afraid of this country suffering from cheap goods. Sir Frederick Williams-Taylor -and I am sure my friends to my right will take his word, he is not a farmer by any means-made the statement the other day that prosperity cannot return to Canada until agriculture becomes prosperous.
Now I want to say a few words about wheat farming. I went down to that mining banquet to-day, and I wondered just on what terms I was there as a guest, and it struck me that perhaps I might be there as a wheat miner; but really I was not there in that capacity. We have very often heard the expression used in this House with regard to the wheat farmers of the West, that they are "wheat miners." I do not want to make any harsh statements about any members of the House, but I think my friends will admit that when they look over to this
part of the House and talk of the wheat miner, it is not very complimentary, to say the least. What is wrong with wheat production? Are we not all anxious to see how the wheat crop in the West is prospering, and how many million bushels are going to come East to grease the wheels of industry? Then why pour contempt on those who are producing that wheat? Mr. Speaker, the people who talk that way do not understand the conditions that have existed in western Canada during the opening up of that great country. It would have been an utter impossibility for that country to be opened up if wheat had not been produced in large quantities, and produced easily. flnat is how that country has been opened up, and that production is responsible for the factories that have been built in eastern Canada to supply agricultural implements to the people who are engaged in raising the wheat. I believe that for many, many years to come wheat growing is to be the one great industry of the three western prairie provinces. I have no hesitation in saying that, and it is no use talking of "wheat miners" in a contemptuous sort of way. If hon. members would only consider what it means to start and fertilize 640 acres-it might be possible to fertilize a five or ten or twenty acre farm -but when farming is conducted on the large scale on which it had to be conducted in the early process of opening up the West, it would be an utter impossibility. Wheat farming, while it does to a certain extent rob the soil, is an absolute necessity in opening up that country and building up industry there. It is that which enables the farmer to build his home and outbuildings, and buy his implements and all the other articles he needs to carry on production. In process of time, of course, there will be change. As I said before, changed conditions require changed methods, and in our older province of Manitoba a change is gradually taking place now, and no doubt in the future there will be more diversified farming carried on.
This brings me to say just a few words with regard to credit. I have not yet had the opportunity of reading Dr. Tory's report in regard to agricultural credits, and I have only this to say at the moment: There is a need for credit of some kind that will carry the farmer over from three to five years. I can imagine conditions in southern Manitoba to-day where the farmers who are aware that they cannot count on wheat as a safe crop may be willing to turn to mixed
The Budget-Mr. Forke

farming, and will need credit to carry them over that length of time in order to enable them to engage in more diversified farming. However, I want no credit that is just going to mean an increase of debt. I am perfectly well aware of the fact that in the West credit has been too easy to get in a great many instances, and it would have been a blessing sometimes if farmers had been refused credit when they were seeking it.
Courage is needed to-day by all sections of people in this Dominion. Whether we are engaged in industry, in commerce or in farming, we all need courage to face the difficulties that are ahead of us, and, Mr. Speaker, I cannot but think at the present moment of the rural homes all over this Dominion. When we speak of the standard of living, I certainly do not want to see the standard of living reduced in the rural homes of this country, and I am perfectly sure that my friends to my right who have been speaking so much on behalf of our Canadian manufacturers will fully agree with me in that sentiment. We do not wish to see the standard of living reduced in our rural homes, but that is what is taking place to a very large extent to-day. Out on the prairies-and I speak of the prairies because I know conditions there, though I believe it is the same in other parts of Canada as well-the standard of living has dropped. There is no denying that fact. And if my blood stirs sometimes when I think of it, it is just because I know the conditions. I know what some of the heroic women who have done so much to develop that country have suffered, and it is no playing politics with me, I can assure you. But let us hope that a brighter day is dawning. Nations, must learn, as individuals learn, that they cannot live to themselves alone, that when one prospers all will prosper to a certain extent.
In closing, I think that politically things look brighter to me in this Dominion than they have done for some time past. I think the hard spell is over. But there is one thing I would like to say to the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) in regard to the customs tariff. To be candid, there is something about that dumping clause that I do not like. Something, no doubt, may be said in favour of it, I know it is a complicated question; but it does seem to me to place too much power in the hands of any minister when he is able at any time to enforce a measure of that kind that may actually amount to high protection, if it is not very carefully handled. I do not know

what can be done, but I do hope that the government will have some solution, and that some undertaking will be given to us before we are called upon to put the final seal of our approval upon the budget that is now before the House. I do not think anything can be said in favour of a minister having the power to put this clause in force at any time he chooses. I do not want the Acting Minister of Finance or any other member of the House to think that I am tccusing them of having made a wrong use of this clause; my only object is to save them from themselves, to avoid placing temptation in their way. I hope that something can be done in that respect.
I wish also to say a word in reference to the amendment that has been moved. I am sure that the mover of that amendment (Mr. Woodsworth) is quite sincere, and that his intentions are good. There may be also some in my own party and group who may differ with me in this statement, but I say that the amendment, as moved at that time, was not in the best interests of the movement which we represent in this part of the Chamber. However, that is my own opinion; I am quite willing to let any other person have any different idea which he chooses to have. I suppose there will be a certain amount of what I may call "unholy glee" on the part of some who think this places the Progressives in a rather difficult position. Personally,
I have felt no difficulty whatever. I am conscious that the course I am pursuing is the right course. It has seemed to me that if I voted for the amendment, which in reality would be a vote of want of confidence that I would have to vote against the budget also. That I think would be a mistake under present conditions. I know very well that out in the country-where it takes some time for information to percolate into all the different sections -some people will wonder why I should not be prepared to support an amendment that calls for a reduction of taxation on the necessities of life. However, I am not afraid, Mr. Speaker, but that with time and with full information, and when the whole statement has been received, I shall have the approval of the great mass of the people.
Now, I want to point out why I believe I could not support this amendment. I do not think that it accomplishes anything, I do not believe that it means anything, because it is only a gesture; and no one could suppose for a moment that it is likely to be carried by a majority of this House. On the other hand, there are two clauses in the amendment that I do not approve of, but disapprove of. One clause asks for a tax on unimproved land

The Budget-Mr. Forke
values. Now, I took the. trouble during my campaign in Brandon of sending out hand bills stating that I was opposed to any plank of this kind. Other members of this House may not have done the same. Nevertheless that is my position in regard to that particular plank and my reason for doing so was this. For several years I had equalized the assessments in the province of Manitoba both urban and rural. I knew the actual conditions of property owners in that province. Nowhere did I know of a single individual who would not be willing to sell his land and sell it immediately at the amounts it was assessed at and as a revenue producer this idea was absolutely and utterly useless-as far as Manitoba was concerned any way.
In regard to succession duties let me say this. The province of Manitoba has a succession duty at the present time and I would be opposed to the Dominion entering into that field until there had been a conference between the federal and the provincial authorities as to the boundaries of taxation. I do believe that such a conference ought to take place, and that there should be no overlapping in this matter of taxation. The boundaries should be clearly fixed showing where the Dominion or the provinces should enter this field. But the provinces are in the field now. They need that amount of revenue and I think they ought to have it. I have spoken in this manner because I really do not know the exact position of all the members in this part of the House upon that question. Each member can vote to suit himself; if he does so there will be no re-[DOT] criminations, there will be no faultfinding. I believe that when a man acts according to his conscience he can always justify his actions.
I have already said that so far as we are concerned there will be no turning back. We have our faces toward the rising sun, and we are seeking to clear away the barriers of special privilege and afford equal opportunity to all. Since I commenced speaking some hon. members have' alluded ?;:>
bargains that have been made. I want to make the statement clearly and without an;r equivocation of any sort that I am under no obligation to any other group in this House, save and except the group that has done me the honour of electing me as its leader and has given me its friendship and its support. I utterly deny and repudiate the idea that there has been any bargaining, or any dealing of any kind whatever, between the members' of this group and those of any other group in this House. I made the statement at the commencement of the present session that the - government
would get the support of the Progressives when they brought in progressive measures. This has been twisted and used in newspapers in all directions, and by hon. members to my right, to prove that I had made some arrangement with the government in regard to their support. I make exactly the same statement to-day that I did on the former occasion- if the government bring in progressive measures they will get Progressive support.
With this statement I shall close my remarks. I have faith in Canada. I have faith that in the future we are going to solve our difficulties. But if there are any in this House who believe that the day of the progressive movement is over in Canada they are badly mistaken. Great changes have taken place all over the world. We have a Labour government in Great Britain to-day.

speechtext: Just have patience. We can look forward to changes in the country to the south of us. I am not a prophet but I predict that there will be vast changes in the economic and political life in the great republic to the south of us in the not distant future. We, Mr. Speaker, have reached no standing place in this movement at the present time. As I have already said our faces are toward the rising sun, and we are going to march forward unafraid. WTe are not going to go back into past history and say that what happened forty years ago must be maintained to-day. We realize that mankind has not made a very good job in the conduct of the world during the last century. When we think of conditions as we find them; when we look at Europe and think of the misery, the degradation, and the sufferings that have occurred, the tremendous blunders that man, in his so-called wisdom, has made in the government of the world, do we feel satisfied that we are moving just as we ought to move? Are we afraid of making some step forward? Mr. Speaker, I look to the future hopefully, and I am not afraid to step forward and to enter upon new and untrodden paths.
