speechtext:
I notice that
on page J56 of Hansard he said with regard to the tariff :
I have heard our friends the protectionists state, and they had no hesitation in stating, that if we adopted a tariff policy higher than it is now, a policy somewhat similar to that which they have in the United States-although it does not seem to work very well there so far as the farmers are concerned- it would work splendidly here, it would stop emigration, would increase immigration, would give more employment, would raise wages, would raise the price of farm products, and at the same time decrease the cost of living. I think they are too modest in the advantages which they claim their tariff would accomplish. Would it not also cure earache and headache, lumbago and sciatica, remove dandruff and prevent the hair from falling out? Mrs. Lydia Pink-ham's pills would be nowhere alongside an adequate tariff, which, in the estimation of these gentlemen, would be a tariff made up by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association.

The Budget-
-Mr. Garland (Carleton)
I might say in passing that, being a druggist, I would remind the hon. gentleman that Lydia Pinkhnm's pills are usually recommended for female ailments, and therefore do not apply to this side of the House. But I presume that when he delivered his speech he had taken some of these pills, or was badly in need of them.
With regard to the boasted economy of this government, I cannot as yet see that any economy is being practised by it. We had an item in the Public Works estimates asking for an expenditure of one and a quarter million dollars for the acquisition of the Colonial building in London, England, and another three-quarters of a million dollars expenditure on alterations for the same building. At the time I said that this two million dollars might have been spent to much better purpose in our own city in making the "deserted village" between here and the buildings within the next quarter of a mile appear as if the government owned the land. Instead of taking this course and providing suitable accommodation for various government departments, the administration continues to rent buildings from those who are friendly towards it at election times.
The government also boast of the retrenchment they have effected by reducing the number of civil servants. But I notice that in every case the dismissals are of those in the lower grades. I have yet to find that any of the high-salaried men have been dismissed, whereby some benefit to the country might result. Of course, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock) told the unfortunate ones, "We are going to use you well; we have employed you for about nineteen years, and we are going to give you two months' pay when we dismiss you." He, a friend of Labour, would so treat loyal employees after such a length of service!
I am surprised to know that 'last year over five hundred of our technical men reft the service. I am also surprised to know that the members of the technical staff in the Department of Agriculture are not paid the same as are similar staffs in other branches. This, Mr. Speaker, I think is one of the reasons why there is so much discontent in the service to-day. I have already expressed the opinion that the same amount of bonus should be paid to every person who is doing similar work whether he has dependents or not, for undoubtedly civil servants working beside each other and doing the same amount of work should be paid the same remuneration. Nothing is likely to benefit the Civil
Service more than a contented staff. We do not need to go outside this building to find that some of the lower grades, such as those engaged in the char service, have not yet received their current bonus. These are the very people who are most in need of the bonus, and it should be paid to them without
delay.	.
Now a word with respect to the retirement fund established in 1898. This is made up of 5 per cent deductions from the salaries of civil servants; the government do not contribute to the fund at all. According to a return brought down recently, the government had on hand on the 31st March, 1922, to the credit of the retirement fund 88,680,112.76. Now, on the amounts so deducted the government pays only 5 per cent half yearly; but at the same time they do not mind floating Victory bonds and paying those who purchase them practically 7 per cent. I consider that the 5 per cent interest should be raised, for the fund is at the disposal of the government and can be made use of from time to time for national purposes.
With regard to the Superannuation biff,
I heartily agree with the principle, but I defer dealing with this until the measure- is before us for discussion in the committee stage.
One of the most lamentable things that is taking place in this country is our immigration. In answer to a question I placed on the order paper I was informed that the government spent in 1923, 890,171.50 for officials and employees of the immigration staff in the United States, placed there, it must be, to bring immigrants from that country into Canada. I do not know what results have been obtained, but we are led to believe that our people are leaving this country at the rate of about 500 a day, if that is so, there is an excellent opportunity for the government to save 890,000 a year by withdrawing their immigration staff from the United States.
With regard to the policy adopted by the government of bringing immigrants to this country, I believe that there is plenty of room within the borders of Canada for ten times the population we have to-day. I would like to see more people brought from the British Isles, and it would be well in bringing them over to bring some who have money that they can spend on factories and the like to give employment to those who come here. The hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) is going to buy a double disc harrow so that he can do twice as much work with one teamster as he did before;
165S

The Budget-Mr. Denis (St. Denis)
that is the way he is going to help labour. We are bringing Mennonites into this country. There is room for them all but I think we should try first to get people from the British Isles. We should have, to my mind, a restricted immigration. When the party of the present administration was previously in power they brought to Canada large consignments of Doukhobors and settled them on the best lands of the West. And what has happened? Last year t.he Doukhobors went back in a body to their own country, with millions of Canadian dollars in their pockets. They lived, in this country, they were fed in this country, they were protected in every wa3q during the war and otherwise; they were even clothed by the government. Now, if a man has five or six sons in On-, tario, for instance, and he wants to move to the West, he would not get from any government, a railroad ticket to take bim two miles, but to my mind these are the people to whom we ought to give some encouragement-the young boys from Ontario or the provinces further east who have been brought up on the farm. It is unfortunate that the only thought we who are bringing up sons can have to-day is that they are being brought up to become residents of the republic to the south; we cannot see any prospects for a boy in this country. The result is that our young men are going to the United States. A lot of them will come back, but the intelligent, bright young men who go there and make good will remain there; we are really getting only the second rate fellows back. In twenty-five j'ears from now our neighbours to the south will have got all the cleverest men that this country produces.
I do not know that I can say anything further, except that the only consistent course I can follow is to vote against this budget.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The economic policy, Mr. Speaker, which the present government has been carrying . out, ever since they have been at the helm of public affairs, has produced excellent results. The financial statement which has just been submitted to us by the hon. Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), allows us to hope for happier days; it assures us that the administration is in better hands, and that, no doubt, we are on the road to prosperity. For my part, Sir,
I am quite satisfied with the budget that file hon. minister has brought down. It answers the wishes of the great majority of citizens of this country, and also responds to their needs. It is the return to the old-time 
and distinctive policy of the Liberal party, the policy to which the country is indebted for its great prosperity in the past.
What is very pleasing to note in this jrnar's budget, is the decrease of the national debt which, under the old Conservative regime, had enormously increased, rising from $340,042.052.03, in 1911 to $2,340,878,983.09 in 192122, the last year of an unfortunate Conservative administration, and, without precedent in the annals of our history. The administration of public affairs wars under the present government during only the three last months of that fiscal year; consequently, the responsibility for that year's administration rests with the late government. In that year, the national debt increased to $2,422,135,801.73. In 1922-23, the first year of the present regime, the debt increased to $2,453,776,868.74, however, for the year 1923-24 ending March 31, the present government have announced that the debt has been reduced to $2,410,162,174.
The heritage which the late government bequeathed to the present one was not much to be envied. However, inspired by the greatest fortitude and a most determined patriotic desire, they courageously buckled down to work. The whole country, to-day, rejoice in seeing that work accomplished for the general welfare of its citizens. To reach such a result, Sir, a strict economy had to be carried out in the administration of public affairs and certain pressing work postponed, such for instance, as the erection of a post office in my constituency, the need of which has been felt for a number of years, and which I have continually been requesting since I had the honour of respresenting the division of St. Denis. This post office is needed, owing to the large increase of population, the commercial and industrial expansion and especially the importance this northern section of the city of Montreal has taken within the last years; it is to-day the most beautiful part of the great metropolis of Canada. Its population is considerable, having over 100,000 inhabitants, and, within a few years, it will reach 125,000. It is the most favourable locality to reside in, both as regards the sanitary and financial standpoint. It is by practising economy, Sir, that the government have succeeded in bringing down the expenses and increasing the revenues to such an extent that, this j'ear, they were able to announce to the country a surplus of $67,750,000. We must rejoice in seeing such results and congratulate the government on this success. I do not ask our friends who sit on your left, Sir, to do

The Budget-Mr. Denis (St. Denis)
so; let them, however, cease sowing falsehoods and slanders throughout the country and especially in Quebec, and, instead of spreading the whisper of death, let them breathe the air of prosperity which the present administration is sowing. I think, Sir, that this air does not suit them accustomed as they are to live in an atmosphere contaminated by all kinds of parasites from whach the country has suffered during their administration.
The most serious side of our opponents' criticism, is the reproach of our having disturbed the tariff and having been false to our last year's pledge of upholding its stability. Whatever they may think,. say or read, they cannot possibly prove such a contention. This government promised to give the country a tariff according to its needs and conditions. Under present circumstances, there are two classes which are in need of protection: The labouring class, which constitutes the large majority of consumers, and the farming class whose industry is threatened, owing to the prevailing low prices of their products and the high cost of implements and the expense of farming. Briefly, the government wished to grant the small wage-earners, the labouring class, as much protection as is offered to the wealthier classes. It is with that aim in view that the government has. reduced the sale tax by one per cent. This reduction may appear to us very small, on first sight, but for those who have a large family, tjiis is quite an item at the end of the year. We find these large families especially among people of small means, workmen, farmers, and not among the rich. The former supply the state with man power which is far more valuable than money, especially in a country like ours, whose natural resources are so rich and abundant, and await but strong hands to develop and make them productive for the state. Similarly, we should be very thankful to the government for its decision to raise the income exemption from $300 to $500 for each child under 18 years of age. It is the duty of the government to promote in every way an increase in the birth-rate, throughout the country by giving the greatest possible protection to those patriotic people. The country needs an increase in population. Immigration contributes to a certain extent, but we should favour the increase which comes from births rather than from immigration. It sometimes happens-and it is a misfortune-that these foreign immigrants have not all the qualifications necessary to
become good Canadian citizens, for instance, those who are sent from reformatories or other institutions of the kind. I would ask the government to be very particular. Canada must not be looked upon as a dumping ground. There is plenty of place here for all good citizens desirous of settling in this country and becoming good Canadians. Blood ties must not be considered in the selection of immigrants, but what must be especiall}' taken into account is their turn of mind, character and their manhood.
What pleased me very much was to find, in the budget, the lowering of duty on farming implements and the disappearance of the sale tax on said articles. Agriculture is the first and most important of our national industries. It is certainly in need of a little more protection. The government became aware of this and I therefore congratulate them. Let us help to make our farmers prosperous, let us increase their purchasing power and I am convinced that the other industries will feel its good effects. As to manufacturers in general, I think they have no cause for alarm. This government has no intention to hinder them in getting a reasonable profit out of their industries, its aim is simply to help those who are in need, and it requests the manufacturers not to be too selfish, but content themselves with what is reasonable and just. In my humble opinion what is detrimental to the industries of a country is the decrease of the purchasing power of a people. When money is plentiful, we buy; when it is the reverse, business is :at a standstill. Protection which can but increase the cost of manufactured products, cannot be the remedy. The secret of a good government is to find the means of increasing this purchasing power. It is the foundation of success. I am convinced that the present government will attain this end.
I had no intention, Sir, of detaining the House very long, but I cannot resume my seat without making a few remarks on the construction of the Hudson Bay railway. I am rather astonished, considering our financial situation, to note that our friends the Progressives are asking for the building of this railway which would require a large expenditure. It is true that our financial situation has somewhat improved, however, we must not undertake further outlays without being very sure that they are in the general interest of the country. I think that this railway construction would be a pure loss for Canada, the open season is too short and ice floes block the Hudson strait during almost
1660	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Denis (St. Denis)
the whole year, with the exception of July and August when it is too early to make use of this route for the transportation of grain. I base my statement on reports made by people having lived the year around in those parts, and therefore, well acquainted with the subject. This railway is not to be looked upon as a luxury, but as a means of communication required for the needs of the population and their trade; it is too expensive an undertaking to be left to the whims of any one. The Hudson Bay railway will not remedy the situation from which the western farmers suffer, such as the high rates of freight and insurance. I would advise them to postpone their request, this would save a great deal of money to the country and would avoid placing a new burden on the people.
I shall close my remarks, Sir, by assuring the government of my entire trust in them. I urge them to continue, their Liberal policy and I feel convinced that the country will be grateful to them when the hour for reward has struck. Our friends who sit on your left, Sir, will once more be disappointed, and it will not be the last time.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not often I take up much of the time of the House, and I am sorry that there are not more hon. members in their seats. No one can accuse me of taking up a great deal of time, and I ask the indulgence of the House this afternoon to bring before it the agreement between the city of Toronto, the Toronto Harbour Commission, the railways and this government in connection with the viaduct.
You are all aware that a representative delegation came down from Toronto on a special train recently and met the Prime Minister and the cabinet in the Railway Committee room. It was a very large and harmonious delegation representing the Toronto Board of Trade, the Toronto City Council, the School Board, and several other organizations which it is not necessary to mention.	The delegation asked that the
government honour the agreement entered ;nto in 1913 between the Canadian Pacific Railway, the Grand Trunk Railway, and the city of Toronto. I am sorry the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and t'he Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) are not present. The reception the delegation got was a very fair one, but the reply to the demands made by the city of Toronto was not just what the city expected to get. The Prime Minister said that he was having difficulty in battling his estimates through

parliament, and that no matter how friendly the government might feel towards carrying out this agreement, parliament had to vote the money, and so tonight I wish to draw the attention of parliament to this agreement. That is why I am sorry there are not more hon. gentlemen in their seats.
I have not been asked to bring this matter before parliament by the city of Toronto, but as I was an old member of the city council at the time these negotiations were going on, between 1908 and 1913, and was chairman of the Board of Works and of the Property Committee of the council, I felt it was my duty to bring this matter before parliament.
Before 1908 the city was in negotiation with the railways demanding an elevated track along the waterfront, and in 1908 the Board of Railway Commissioners issued instructions that the tracks should be elevated. The railways opposed that order and appealed to the Privy Council. They lost their case before the Privy Council, and then they began sparring for time until 1913, when they came forward with a proposition of their own and submittted it to the city of Toronto. The city of Toronto came to an agreement with the Grand Trunk and the Canadian Pacific in that year, and the agreement was signed, sealed and delivered, and approved by the railway board. All interests were satisfied, and the city of Toronto thought they were going to have the viaduct built right away. But another year passed and then the war came in 1914. We all know that the government and the city had their hands full as soon as the war came, and the city of Toronto did not then press for the viaduct. After the war came the collapse of the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific, and then finally the taking over of all these roads by the government. The Canadian Pacific has signified its willingness to go ahead with the agreement; Sir Henry Thornton has also signified that he sees his way clear to going ahead with it; and now it is up to parliament to vote the money so that the government can carry out their share of the agreement.
Some people may ask, what is the necessity for this viaduct? I am going to give to parliament the facts that make it necessary that this viaduct should be built. The whole waterfront is cut off from the city by level crossings. Unfortunately, in the early days of Toronto, when it was a small town called " Muddy Little York "-you know how a railway will come into a small town, and how on every occasion it gets the best part of the town or city, and that is what hap-

The Budget-Mr. Spence
pened in the early days in Toronto. The railways built along the waterfront, and they have to have room to develop. At present they are a hindrance to the development of the city, because they occupy the whole waterfront and the city cannot get access to its industrial areas along that waterfront. There are twenty-two level crossings in this territory that is supposed to be covered by the viaduct. In 1908, I think it was, the Grand Trunk and the city went in together and depressed the tracks from Sunnyside to Bathurst street. Hon. members who have been to the Toronto Exhibition may remember how in the old days they had to cross the tracks to get there, and how nowadays they can walk right into the grounds, the tracks being below. The viaduct will carry out this scheme in the other end of the city. There are fifty main line tracks, averaging more than two at each crossing, and every now and again an accident happens at one of these crossings. There are sixty-nine shunting tracks in the twenty-two crossings, averaging more than three to a crossing. In the summer time we have a wonderful boat business in and out of the city of Toronto, and all inward and outward waterbound freight has to cross these tracks; you can understand what that means.
At these particular crossings theie are from ten to twelve tracks. These have to be crossed in order to reach the coal sheds, elevators, foundries, and fruit warehouses on the waterfront. The whole of the fruit shipments that come across the lake have to be carried across these level crossings, and with the amount of railway traffic that is going on it is a very dangerous proposition. All tourist and passenger traffic to the waterfront must cross these tracks, and the unfortunate thing is that at eight or nine o'clock in the morning, one o'clock in the afternoon, and other hours, when thousands of people are streaming down to the waterfront, trains of the Canadian Pacific railway, and of the Canadian National railway are apt to be coming in or going out on the tracks. It can readily be seen how dangerous these crossings are. Let me give a definite illustration: A man and his wife, accompanied by three or four children come down to reach the waterfront. A train commences to pass and the family get separted. The wife may get safely across but the watchman stops the husband and children. It results in the greatest inconvenience and causes justifiable alarm. Never a day passes but there is a rush to get across to the waterfront before the trains come along and the wonder is that serious accident do not happen.
It is not uncommon for parties of eight or ten persons to be separated, and for those first across to start off in one boat while those held back have to sail on the later one. Such are the conditions which prevail, and these conditions the city of Toronto want to have eliminated as far as possible. There are boats catering to the tourist and passenger traffic which leave the waterfront of Toronto bound for the Thousand Islands, Montreal, Quebec and the Saguenay. Boats also leave for Hamilton, Niagara Falls, Port Dalhousie and other points. Then there is Toronto island to which the people of the city gain access from the waterfront. Part of the island is occupied by the residences of people who go there for the summer, the balance is devoted to providing entertainment for the masses. To the crowds thronging to Toronto island these crossings are a menace and a great source of inconvenience. Surely hon. members can easily see the necessity for the construction of this viaduct. I have been engaged in the fruit business on the waterfront of Toronto for thirty years, and I have had to cross these tracks many times each day. It is heartrending to see the danger which is incurred, and the delay which people suffer, owing to the movement of trains over these crossings. It is absolutely necessary that some relief measures should be provided.

Well, if I lost a quarter of the time consumed by my hon. friends to my left I would be ashamed of myself. I have not talked more than an hour this session, but I think I have said just as much as some of my hon. friends to my left who have talked a week. I repeat, something should be done to stop the waste of time in this House. For instance, something should be done to discourage the introduction of such radical resolutions as have been submitted by my hon. 'friends to my left. Why, it is ridiculous. I may just instance three. First the resolution to amend the British North America Act. It amounted to nothing but talk-talk and more talk, and every hon. gentleman knew ' what the result would be. The next was to amend the Criminal Code. The third was to do away with capital punishment. What do you think of such resolutions as

those? Do you think it is fair that the country should keep a bunch of men, supposed to have a certain amount of ability, in this House discussing radical resolutions that do not amount to anything at all? I do not know how the government tolerates such a condition of affairs. If I were the government I would do something to stop the introduction of such resolutions.

speechtext:
I am not touching church
union.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I am a strong believer in protection. I want all my friends to my left to understand that.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
"Moderate" or
"adequate?"

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Oh, I am always for moderate protection; that is perfectly all right. I am a strong believer in a protective tariff, and I am more convinced than ever, after watching our neighbours to the south, that we need a higher tariff rather than a lower in order to protect the tillers of our soil and our industries. I want to protect my hon. friends to my left, the tillers of our soil, because I have endeavoured to make my living from them during the last thirty-five years, and I have succeeded fairly well. The reason we need protection is what I will now explain. My hon. friends to my left do not know much about it, and I am going to try to enlighten them. The other night the hon .member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) said: You will never go broke getting a bargain. I reply: No, but the man who gives the bargain goes broke. And that is what my hon. friends would like: everybody would be broke but themselves.
Climatic conditions on the American side operate as a substantial protection to the people there who grow fruit and truck produce of all kinds. In the south they can raise from one to three crops a year while it takes our farmers all their time to raise one crop- and they growl while they are doing it. Take in the southern states,-Florida, Louisiana, Tennessee, Texas, North and South Carolina and Maryland

! will guarantee that the farmers there can raise from two to three crops a year. And yet you are trying to compete with them without protection! Why, it is absolute rot. Take the north shore of Virginia, where prdbably 50,000 acres are under cultivation to potatoes, which supply this country from the beginning of May to the beginning of July. That crop is sold here when the price is good, but when it

The Budget-Mr. Spence
drops the Virginia farmers cease shipping. Then in July I have often sold them carloads of old potatoes, which they plant, and the resultant crop supplies their home market. Can you do that in Canada?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is not patriotic.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What is not patriotic? It
is patriotic to make money wherever you can. What I mean by that, Mr. Speaker, is this:	If the Americans, being wise to the
situation, can grow two crops each year, they are doing right. It is better for them to so apply themselves rather than sit up growling as you gentlemen do. Free trade might help the western farmers temporarily, but it would kill them in the end, as it would also the truck farmers of this country. For free trade would drive away our population, free trade would shut up our industries and the population would leave the urban centres. Take an area within twenty miles of Hamilton-I would talk of Toronto, because I know you gentlemen do not like to hear of that city Suppose one of the big industries there should close down, it would throw out of employment four thousand people-and we anticipate this will happen-and the shutting down of that industry would affect associated industries, and they too would have to close down. As a result the population of Hamilton would soon be reduced from 110,000 to
50,000.	This may actually occur, because a free trade policy is bound to bring about such a result if it does nothing else. My hon. friend here (Mr. Senn) is a truck farmer and lives within twenty miles of Hamilton. He does not do any growling. On the contrary, he is bringing in his produce and finding a ready market for it in Hamilton, for the city has a population sufficient to consume all the fruit and garden truck grown within forty miles of its boundaries. But what is going to happen when we depopulate this urban centre? What are we going to do? Land will drop in value fifty per cent, because the price of land fluctuates with the price of farm products. You gentlemen need a little more experience. Your mind is too narrow; you are continually thinking of yourselves to the exclusion of everybody else.
Now, let me tell you something of the class of people you have to deal with in the United States. You gentlemen to my left are continually talking about the great market to the south. I will tell you how selfish the people are there. I happen to be in the nursery business. In 1917, for the purpose
of improving their own nursery industry- and I would approve of Canada doing the very same thing-when the United States government saw that the nursery business was being hampered by an over supply of nursery imports from Holland, England and France, they put on a high duty; but they were not content with this, and the next year they put on an embargo, shutting out nursery imports altogether, thus encouraging their own people to propagate nursery stock They have also protected their grape growers; they have forced the people to eat nothing but California grapes, which is the right thing to do,
I would recommend the same course for adoption by the Canadian government under similar circumstances, for protection is the only thing. They put an embargo on Spanish grapes, thus preventing the people eating a better grape in order to force them to eat the California product, which is good enough for them. What do we do in this country?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We have a good
government.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, we will not say we
have a good government. We reduced the duty on wine through the French treaty and killed our grape growers-an entirely different thing from what the United States did with their grape growers. We killed ours; they built theirs up.
Now, I am going to say something else that our hon. friends may think radical, too. As I said before, I am a great believer in protection, and I am a great believer in raising money in the cheapest possible way, that is, by customs tariff. To-day we have entirely too much direct taxation, entirely too many kinds of taxation. We have taxation municipal, provincial and federal, and the condition is such that it would poison the mind of the best citizen against any government. I say there are too many systems of taxation, and they are irritating and annoying everybody. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler) told us of an instance just before the war when the revenue of this country was $136,000,000. At that time they raised $126000,000 by customs tariff and only $1,000,000 in a direct way; to-day we are raising over $155,000,000 by customs tariff and $199,000,000 by taxation, which is absolutely unfair. You are hitting the people who are trying to make an honest dollar, to accommodate and please somebody else.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Who pays the taxes?
The Budget-Mr. Spence

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Everybody knows who
pays them. You do not get much out of the farmer, though he is entitled to everything that is coming to him, and if you can find a farmer in Ontario between Toronto and Niagara falls south or from that down east who will say an unkind word about me, I will buy you a good treat. I have farmer friends all over Ontario and I am willing to help them in every way I can. If my hon .friends, however, cannot see what is good for them I am going to point it out to them.
Lower the tariff on anything, I do not care what it is, and you kill industry. I will just mention three or four commodities by wav- of illustration. There is barbed wire, for instance. At one time there was a duty of | cents on it, but now the duty has gone forever. Cream separators could be made in this country, but no duty is imposed on them and to-day they are made in the United States. Binder twine-that is a thing that touches the farmer; he is always talking about binder twine; the duty was taken off binder twine and what happened? Before the duty was taken off we had twenty-three factories in Canada turning out binder twine, now we have three, and the price has gone up from 7 and 8 cents a pound to 15 cents a pound. That is the result of taking the duty off and killing your industry. That is what will happen if you drive your farm implement people out of Canada: they will go back to the States and say "Now, we will make you pay for your implements; you will pay it all back with good interest."

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If my hon. friend will permit a question, may I ask, what is the output of the three twine factories now compared with the total output when there were twenty-three factories operating?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
One-third, I presume. I
must say that I had not looked into that, but I am informed on reliable authority-by an hon. gentleman to my left here-that one-third of what we use is made in this country. That is the trouble with the farmer in the West: He has got his eye southward; for goodness' sake let him get it the other way. They seem to be satisfied, now that they have killed the woollen mills, killed more industry and made it more difficult to sell their products. They have killed the home market, which was one of the best markets, after all- and after a while I will tell you something which will make you understand why. You have killed the farm implement business, at least, you have started on the way, and next year the truth of what we are saying now will 
be shown. That was the case with the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin) in his remarks on the French treaty:	He told the
House last year what would happen and this year he showed them what had happened. What he said last year was true, and what he said this year was true.
I am a believer in economy. Personally I have always been accustomed to economy. I am not like some people; I was not born with a silver spoon in my mouth, and I have always had to consider economy. I like to see economy practised by the government or a municipality just as I practise it in my own business, but there are very few here who look at it that way or they would not talk so long and so often. Our overhead has increased in this country by leaps and bounds, increased out of all proportion to population. It is caused by too much legislation, too much social welfare, too much spoon feeding of the individual, killing initiative and causing indolence in the country. Is that not right? I think my hon. friends really agree with me but they have not got the backbone to say it. We (have heard about widows' pensions, mothers' pensions and old age pensions, but recently we have heard of a new one. the "out of work pension." That was applied in the Old Country, and I heard somebody here advocate the same thing. Just imagine an out of work pension in Canada-why, nobody would ever work; in fact, lots of them do not work now. I heard of an instance in Ireland where you got 27 shillings when you were out of work as against 35 when you worked-now, who would work?
I do not believe even my hon. friends to my left would work under those conditions.
We have too many fads introduced into parliament, too many dreamy ideas, too much nonsense all the time. Legislators, representatives of the people, should have backbone, but as my old friend Sam McBride of the city of Toronto would say, the difficulty with legislators is that their wishbone is where their backbone should be.
Another way of economizing is by cutting out all commissions investigating this and that, costing $300,000 for this, $500,000 for that, and so on. Members of parliament should be in a position to accept their share of the responsibility for the government of this country and no commission should be appointed outside of this House. You can get men in this House who are just as capable of investigating anything as you can get outside of it, and in that way you will save the country money. I have always advocated, that; in the city council I did the same

The Budget-Mr. Spence
thing, so it is nothing new for me. I never yet saw anything come out of a commission; they are usually told the finding, they bring it before you, and that is all there is to it.
We have too many publications coming from the Printing Bureau, and I would advise the government to look into this very thoroughly with a view to seeing what could be eliminated. There is an extravagant waste of paper; the mail carriers of this country are loaded down with useless material. Seventy-five per cent of what the mail carriers carry around in the city of Toronto is junk that nobody ever reads. My cellar is full of it and every other cellar is full of it in the same way. Unfortunately we cannot bum it because we use oil burners. When we used to burn, coal we could dispose of the stuff, but to-day it is piling up and we have not even anybody to sell it to. I saw in Hansard a question asked by the hon. member for North Wellington (Mr. Pritchard) in this connection, and it was a good question; it brought out some information. He asked:
1.	How many tons of waste paper have been sold by the government during the last fiscal year?
2.	What is the total amount received for same?
3.	What per cent of this amount was obtained by the Department of Agriculture?
The Hon. Mr. Copp answered the first two questions. In reply to the first he said:
The weight of paper sold is not available.
That is information for youl Just imagine a department with a head giving that out. The answer to the second was: $497.36. Well, that is pretty good. The answer to the third question was:
Does not refer to this department.
As usual, no information from the Department of Agriculture. The question was also answered with relation to the Post Office Department, as follows:
1.	350.
2.	$4,199.65.
3.	No information.
With respect to the Department of Public Printing and Stationery-and here is where the extravagance comes in-this was the answer:
1.	722 tons, 1,509 pounds.
2.	$26,558.30.
Now, this is a serious proposition. It is extravagance, and no matter what government is in power, no matter whether this has been going on for the last half century or not, it should stop, and now is the time to stop it. I presume that half of that amount scrapped was never sent out, but was just baled up as waste paper.

speechtext:
Is the hon. member
aware that those figures for the Printing Bureau cover all the waste paper from all the departments of the government in Ottawa, and that the price received is for all the waste paper from every department of the government, not from the Printing Bureau alone?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Post Office Department sold over $4,000 worth, so they must have sold that independently.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is for waste paper at Brockville and other outlying points shipped into Ottawa to be sold.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Anyhow, I think hon. members will agree with me that it is the height of extravagance, and I do not care if my own party were in power I would say the same thing. But you are in power, and it is up to you to remedy it. You would almost think there were good times in the country from the way money is wasted; but when you want any money for something useful there is no money. Last year we bought the Hotel Scribe in Paris, which we did not need, for which we have absolutely no use, for $1,300,000, and now we understand it cost $2,500,000, andithe manipulator, Mr. Aronovici that we heard so much about-well, there is always a fellow in between. My friends to my left object to the middleman. I do not like middlemen in this case, and that is what Mr. Aronovici was. I saw in a paper that came to my office to-day that they expect to spend another $2,500,000 on that Hotel Scribe, so it may take $5,000,000 altogether. I cannot say whether the report is true or not. At all events we know that it has cost in the neighbourhood of $3,000,000, and we know that everything of this kind that is purchased by a government or a municipality always costs more than the original estimate.
Then we have our friend the High Commissioner in London whom I know well-full of vanity as an egg is full of meat. He is of the opinion that he wants a beautiful building in London with a great big stone front, and the great "I Am" walking up into it. Just imagine spending that amount of money there. If the Salada Tea had made it all, I would not mind so much, but the poor taxpayer has to pay for it.
Now I come round to home, to my friends from the West. Ten years ago there were no industries in the West at all. Very little of anything was raised there except wheat. I do. not think there was any dairying done there ten years ago, perhaps five years ago.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What I am going to tell you, you may not know. Yes, even five years ago,
The Budget-Mr. Spence

and I want to compliment the people of Alberta and Saskatchewan for the way they have developed dairying out there. Their cheese factories are doing splendidly. Their creamery butter is first class; they are producing the best make of b'itter in the Dominion right in the province of Alberta; I know what I am talking about, b< cause I am associated with people who are dealing in butter. Alberta is to be congratulated on the splendid make of butter she is turning out,-and as some hon. member has said, the whole country will have to do the same before the butter situation will be as it should be in this country. About five years ago people from the East, people that I know, shipped poultry and cheese and butter, condensed milk and everything into those provinces. But to-day we are receiving in the East, in Toronto and Montreal, hundreds of carloads of butter and cheese from those provinces, and this year alone Alberta and Saskatchewan shipped to the East over a thousands carloads of turkeys, averaging 20,000 pounds to the car. So I say they are to be congratulated. They are developing an industry out there, and in the near future my friends to my left will be howling for protection just as loudly as they are howling to-day for free trade.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What did they get for the turkeys?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: As much as they deserved. That just slipped out; I did not intend to give that answer.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: W7hat did you get out of it?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
To be frank with you, I was good enough to help some of your western friends out with their turkeys. One man came with a carload of turkeys, chickens and eggs, for fifty-six different people, and he had all the stuff from each man packed in one box. I got him a place to put his stuff in, and I sold some of the turkeys for him and it cost him nothing. But that is not the point. The people in the West to-day are aware that they must get proper boxes made to crate their stuff in; they must have proper refrigeration, and kill properly; they must use the proper-sized box. Some have been doing that this year, and they are making a wonderful success of it. This year you have 100,000,000 bushels of wheat in this country more than the world can use, and there is nothing else for it but that wheat must come down in price to create a demand for it. If you drop anything in price you will generally find someone willing to buy it and take a chance on selling it, but I maintain in this 
case he will lose. I paid 35 cents a pound for western turkeys and paid as low as 23 cents, and some of them should never have been shipped. I do not blame my western friends for that, because they are not fully conversant with the class of stuff that will bring the price. But you are developing this industry in the West, and you people will soon be hollering for protection as loudly as you holler now for free trade, and you will remember what I have told you, don't forget that! The eastern provinces cannot afford to let you men in the West think you rule the country no matter how much we think of you, and we certainly entertain a high opinion of you.

I will take that back and
say that you work all day, but you certainly do not work all night. In order to get along in life many men in business have to work practically day and night. I remember when I started-I do not mind telling, I am not ashamed of it-I had a mind to be at the top in my business. I worked all day in the fruit market beginning at seven o'clock in the morning, and at seven o'clock I went to the office and worked there until two and three o'clock every morning. I did that .for three months at a time. I have never been able to get the leisure for a trip across to Niagara. But many of you gentlemen when you work a few months in the spring and fall get an automobile and go off for a hike to Vancouver. You toil not neither do you spin. Now, the point I want to make is this: Take fifty men starting upon the farm and fifty men starting in the retail business, and you will see at the end of ten years the men on the farm will have more money than the men in business. Yet you think business men are better off than you are. I tell you frankly that you have more money than they have. Take any two hundred people in the retail business in the city of Toronto, I doubt whether any fifty of them could square their accounts up.

The Budget-Mr. Spence
The middleman has been accused of being a vulture. I happen to be a middleman myself but I have never been a vulture, or a parasite either. To-day conditions are terrible in this country; business is really bad, and these tariff changes are going to make it worse. The bankers are beginning to make you square up if you happen to have an overhead that amounts to anything. The strong has always protected the weak, and we propose to carry out that policy. In Toronto we have to enact by-laws to prevent people from walking in front of the street cars and killing themselves. Similarly, some of you gentlemen will have to be protected, and we are going to protect you. The difficulty is that hon. members from the prairie provinces think that all the wisdom has been extracted from the rest of the country and deposited in the West. Now that is not so. All the wisdom of Canada is not confined to any part of the country. You in the West have some, we in the East have our share, and the balance belongs to people in some other part of the country. Still hon. gentlemen from the West talk as if they "knew it all" and that we knew nothing. What we require in this country-I am talking seriously-is national unity. We cannot secure that without a real national policy, a policy that will keep Canada for the Canadians, Canadian business for Canadians, but keeping in mind all classes. Let us forget our troubles in future; let us bury the hatchet and help each other. I say to you gentlemen from the West: Stop your growling and get friendly with yourselves. Our population unfortunately is not large; it is a shame that this country is not growing any faster than it is. We really have no internal business, and if we do not retain our population conditions in future will be much worse than they are at present not only for the farmer but for the artisan and the man of business. Mr. Beatty of the Canadian Pacific Railway-he must be a fairly smart fellow, he draws a big salary and must earn it-was asked how it was that the United States enjoyed so much prosperity. He said there was a tremendous prosperity in the United States largely by reason of the internal trade developed in the country and which its enormous population made possible. In Canada our internal trade does not amount to anything. But when that country is filled up our turn will come. The United States will be overstocked shortly and then we shall start in on an era of prosperity, we shall be on the eve of a brighter day.
I was glad to hear the speech the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Lapierre) made
this afternoon. I congratulate him on the optimism he displayed when speaking of the mineral resources of northern Ontario. That is the kind of speech that attracts population to the country, not speeches of a pessimistic character in which there is so much whining and growling. I do not like to hear speeches in this House like that delivered by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote). That hon. gentleman had a magazine-I do not know whether it was the Christian Guardian or the Grain Growers' Guide-but he was quoting a lot of stuff out of it and trying to antagonize the working man, the middleman, and the man who produces pork one against the other. "The producer," he says "is getting only seven cents a pound for pork and according to advertisements you cannot buy the bacon for less than forty-five to fifty-five cents."

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since coming to this House at the opening of the session of 1922, I have been a regular attendant, an attentive listener, and a close observer of all that has taken place up to the present time. Under these circumstances, it is quite natural that one should form his own conclusions and make his own deductions as to the relative merit or demerit of the business transacted in this House. I have reached the conclusion that fully one-half of the time of the House has been wasted in academic discussions that lead nowhere, besides costing the people an immense sum of money. Sessions that have lasted five months could have been reduced to three, and would have furnished ample time to dispose of the real business before the House. Long-drawn out speeches, occupying anywhere from one hour to two and a half and three hours, have been of too frequent occurrence over matters that are of no earthly interest to the country, but which only serve the purpose of satisfying the vanity of certain members who think they are endowed with great oratorical ability.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, it is customary in our Mother parliament for members to seldom occupy more than thirty minutes in the discussion of the weighty problems with which they have to deal. This being the case,

The Budget-Mr. Lovett
surely we in this parliament, would have ample time to present our views on any question in the time limit mentioned. I would therefore suggest, Sir, that from now on this session be made a purely business one, and that outside the ministers of the Crown, the right hon. leader of the opposition, and the leader of the Progressive group, all other members, who really desire economy, who really desire that the business before the House be disposed of in the shortest possible time consistent with good legislation, who really desire to make this a real businesslike session, confine their speeches to not over thirty minutes duration.
Having said this much, permit me to offer my hearty congratulations to the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) and the government, on the wise, sound, and able budget which has been presented to this House; and especially do I wish to congratulate the Acting Minister of Finance on the splendid manner in which he acquitted himself in presenting his first budget. I know its contents cannot be considered healing balm to the official opposition, but on the contrary it has rung the death knell to their hopes of a speedy return to power, for they must know that this budget will be thoroughly acceptable to the Canadian people. It is a straight tilt between the forces of high protection on the one hand and those of low tariff on the other. The line of demarcation is clear and distinct. The cleavage between the two parties is clear cut and well defined. The gauntlet has been thrown down and we on this side of the House are not only anxious but eager to take up the challenge when the time shall have arrived to go to the country and meet our opponents on the battle ground of reduced taxation and lower tariff, confident in the belief that the downward revision of the tariff will again restore to the country an overwhelming measure of prosperity.
There are, I believe, three distinct lines of thought regarding our fiscal policy: One of free trade, ideal in theory, but impracticable at the present time, as every sane and reasonable man will admit; one of high protection, which is the god of the Tory party, and which has been tried out in this country under the so called National Policy, but has been weighed in the balance and found wanting; one of low tariff, which by the bringing down of the present budget, has received a new impetus and called into being a real "national policy," which will be far reaching in effect, placing agriculture and all our other basic industries on a sound footing, and at the same time preserving and fostering our manufacturing industries.
No matter what the tariff policy may be, you will always find our manufacturing friends clamouring for more protection, in spite of the fact that they have been pap fed for years and years. Why, Mr. Speaker, their field of vision is so limited, so self-centered, that they begrudge concessions, no matter how small, to other interests in this country. They are so blinded by selfishness that they overlook the fact that the success, expansion, and development of our basic industries is the one thing essential to the success or failure of our manufacturing concerns. We have, in the budget just brought down, a tariff policy on sound Liberal lines calculated to give all interests in the Dominion a fair deal, and in no instance can it be fairly said that hardships have been inflicted on anyone.
The member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) in his opening remarks previous to adjourning the debate, leaped at once to the front, and in his warrior-like style endeavored to detract from the real significance of the surplus as stated by the acting minister in his budget speech, claiming that ten millions should be credited to the former administration, as it was derived from acknowledged Imperial book debts, which had been pending for a long time, a settlement of which had been recently effected. Perhaps there is something in the hon. member's contention, but in order that the matter shall be fairly understood, let me remind the hon. gentleman that when the Liberal government went out of office in 1911, they left in the treasury a surplus of some thirty millions of dollars, so if the ten millions claimed by him is deducted from the thirty millions left by the former Liberal government there would be a balance of twenty millions. This added to the twenty millions surplus of this year would give a surplus of forty millions, instead of thirty millions as announced in the budget speech. So I think the hon. member will not find much comfort whichever way he takes it. Let me also point out to him and his party, that if this $30,000,000 surplus left by the former Liberal administration had not been sqandered by his government there would not be to-day the same reason for the existing high taxation. The people of this country have no one to blame but the former administration and their friends for the immense burdens they are now carrying, and it has been left to the present government to tackle the most difficult task, to disentangle the most awful mess, and to solve the most complex problems, that have ever faced any government in this country since confederation. But I am proud to say that this government grappled with the task
The Budget-Mr. Lovett

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to associate myself with those who have expressed regret that our Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding) has not been able to present what would have been his eighteenth budget. I wish also to compliment the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) upon the businesslike, lucid and fair budget that he presented to the House. I say fair, because this budget takes the first step that we have had in the direction of a satisfactory reduction in customs duties since I have had anything to do with parliament, and for a long time before that. In fact, it is the biggest step taken in that direction that I know of since I came to Canada. But the budget is not so outstanding or so acceptable for what it does in itself as for what the government have proclaimed in regard to it. Some of the remarks made by some of the ministers on the other side of the House are in my opinion perhaps even more noteworthy than the budget itself, for we have had one minister, the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart), state that he hoped this budget sounded the death knell of protection in Canada. Now that is a significant statement, and we hope that his prophecy will be fulfilled. We as a group are not asking, and the people who have elected us have not asked, for free trade all at once. We have never expressed a wish for absolute free trade all at once, although we believe that we should have our tariff reduced to a revenue tariff basis just as soon as possible, and there are reasons for that.
In my discussion of this subject I think I should take a little different line from what most 'hon. members have taken who have spoken so far in this debate. We have heard it said many times that the United States has prospered wonderfully on account of the tariff that protects her industries. I challenge that statement. I lived in the United States until I was a man of middle age, and I have some knowledge and definite opinions regarding this question of whether the United States has prospered on account of the tariff or in spite of it. My own
opinion, which I will present as well as I can, is that the United States has prospered in spite of the high protection which she has carried. I can remember to as far back as about 1868, soon after the war in that country. The United States was in a bad condition at the end of that war, just the same as we are now, and perhaps their condition was even worse. I have seen people in the United States suffer more from the bad conditions than I have yet seen people in Canada suffer, except perhaps where there has been a drought or some other calamity of that kind. But that is not saying that Canada has done as well as she should have. I do not think she has.
Now I want to give my opinions why I think the United States has reached the state of prosperity she has. The first development that I remember distinctly as a boy in that country was the building of the Union Pacific railway across the western part of the United States. That was followed by the building of a railway across the southern part of the United States, a transcontinental line. Then came the building of the Northern Pacific across the northern part, followed soon after by the building of the Great Northern, another transcontinental line, and all of these went through good country. To be quite frank I think the tariff has had very little to do with the prosperity of the United States up to this time, except at intervals, and there were periods when their tariff bore down very heavily on the people. We are in just a similar period now, with the tariff bearing very heavily on the working and middle classes of this country. To some people it is rather a mystery why Canada has not developed as fast as the United States. It is as old a country as the United States. I do not know so much about the early period after 1868. We knew but little of Canada then in the United States, and we had but little chance to learn about it. All I can do, practically speaking, is to take history and hearsay for what happened in Canada until I came to this country. In the United States after the rebellion we started out to develop a country that was just as big in area as Canada is, although more varied in climate. It was a country rich in all sorts of resources, and we had then a population of from thirty-six to forty million people. Now a country with so many people would have a big advantage over Canada with its seven or nine million people, which is what the population has been since I came to this country twenty-five years ago. I do not know exactly what the population of the
The Budget-Mr. Warner

United States was at that time, but it was somewhere in the neighbourhood of thirty-six to forty million people, and with that number you could develop a country much faster than Canada could be developed with its seven or nine millions. Taking it all round, I do not think the United States is a better country than Canada, but they can raise in some parts of the United States things that we cannot raise. In Canada, producing the things we do, we should have prosperity, but we have had handicaps from which the United States has not suffered to the same extent, on account of her big population to start with. Then the United States adopted a policy of soliciting immigrants from all countries. It got many from the British Isles, and a considerable number from the continent: the people arrived so fast that they undoubtedly helped to develop the country very quickly. But I can remember when the United States was handicapped for labour and also suffered greatly for lack of capital. In the period of which I speak nobody talked of the tariff either promoting or retarding development, and yet the tariff was high all the time. But when depression came we noticed the effect of the tariff as we are noticing it in Canada to-day. During the period of which I speak there were times when the United States had to fall back on what it was producing. In the beginning capital came from England, Scotland and Ireland to a greater degree than from any other country. Capital from the British Isles, from France, and from the rest of Europe, poured into the United States for investment, and development was carried on with this borrowed money. The rate of interest was high but in view of the richness of the country not much thought was taken of that at the time. Development went on rapidly-the development of new lands, the construction of railways to those lands, the establishment of new cities. As I have said a large amount of capital poured into the United States from other countries for these purposes. At the time this development was in progress the people were not dependent on what they produced from the soil. They got capital readily for speculation and for future investment and, naturally, everyone spent money lavishly. And things continued to go on in that way. Well, the population grew enormously, and their markets increased. But I can well remember when the exports to what we called "the Old Country" set the price of all that we raised in the United States, and there were periods when it was very hard to stand the price at home which was fixed by the price put on the

products we exported. And that is just the position that Canada is in to-day. I have known wheat, not always of the best quality when compared with Canadian wheat, to sell as low as thirty and forty cents a bushel, and hogs on foot to go at as low a rate as $1.60 a hundred. This brought about a change in the economic conditions, and people began to wonder what was the matter. They began to see that the tariff was pressing on them unduly. I remember 1873 as the period when people first began finding fault with the tariff. And hard times prevailed then. I do know the tariff was not beneficial in its operation then. In my opinion all that it did was to keep those people in a poverty stricken condition until production of various kinds mostly agricultural could get things going again. At any rate, the fight began against a protective tariff, and many people who had been Republicans and had asked for high protection turned round and voted the other way. The Democrats then took office and they were supposed to be a low tariff party. They did cut the tariff down somewhat but they were much like the governments that we have had in Canada -they kept the general level of the tariff very much the same. But during this period we had bank failures, and great business depression outside of the depression in agriculture. Clothing, implements, and other necessities were hard to buy. It was evident that the tariff did enhance the price of things the people needed, and they began to study the fiscal question and to understand it. In view of these facts I am ill-disposed to accept the argument advanced by some hon. gentlemen in this House, that it was the protective tariff that brought an immense population and great prosperity to the United States. I do not believe for a moment that the tariff had any such effect, and I think I know what I am talking about. The* reasons I have described were rather the cause of the prosperity which came to the country to the south. There was the fact that the United States was a country of great natural resources, there was the restless ambition of her people, and the possibility of easily getting capital to develop the country. I do not say that it was the best possible thing that those people obtained so much borrowed capital, but nevertheless it was an instrument in the rapid development of the country. But the argument of the high tariff policy-and the manufacturing industries profiting by reason of it and thereby giving prosperity to the rest of the country-does not explain the great material advancement of the United States; the facts

The Budget-Mr. Warner
are absolutely the reverse of that. The development of the natural resources of the country, and the cultivation of the soil as the republic grew, made it possible for manufacturers to come in and establish themselves and get a market for what they were manufacturing.
I do not know that there is any need for me to progress any further along that line. I simply wanted to express my opinion regarding the effect of a protective tariff on the United States. It does not follow that what happened in the United States can be duplicated in Canada to-day; there were many more people in that country when its period of great development started from forty to fifty years ago than there are in Canada now. Perhaps I may be pardoned at this stage for telling a story regarding the protectionists in this country and the conditions that prevail in Canada after operation of forty to fifty years of a protective policy. There was a coloured man who quarrelled with the rest of the people in his community. He found considerable fault with all the other people and considered that the blame rested with them and not with himself. Somebody questioned him
10 p.m. about it and he said that he wished everybody but himself were dead. He was asked what he would do then. "Well." he said "I would keep store." Now, it looks to me, after forty or fifty years of high protection in Canada that nearly everybody not engaged in industry has been killed off financially so that they cannot buy the goods the manufacturers are making, and the industrialists are trying to "keep store" when other people are not able to buy.
