speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would the hon. gentlemen be good enough to explain why the farmers in the United States are so much in favour of protection?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, I shall be very glad
to do so. I will answer the question at a little length because I want to reply to it in my own way. When land was high in the United States twenty-five years ago I left the country, I wanted to get away from high priced lands. I came to Canada. I found that things looked good enough for me in Alberta to make the attempt to live there. I found no fault with the country, as far as the conditions were concerned, but I was getting to a point in the United States where I could
not make an income on the money that I had in my land, it would not earn interest on the capital invested; and that condition has been growing worse since that time and is a good deal worse now. I went back to the States about six or seven years ago and I found that land that used to be held at too high a price, $40 to $60 an acre, had risen to $300 and $500 an acre, on account of the boom and the speculation in land, and not because the land could produce that much money. On account of the high price of land, and not understanding what was going to happen, people bought land, and many of them paid down the earnings of a lifetime when they were middle-aged, all the money they could get, on the purchase and when the crisis came after the war and the price of produce went down they were unable to pay for their land, and after having paid all that they had saved up in their lifetime many of them had to leave the land. The price of the land was above its earning power; the land would not pay interest on the investment. Then they turned around and asked for a tariff to protect them against our wheat being brought in there to make good flour for them. Just exactly what has happened in the United States is going to happen in Canada if we do not come to our senses soon enough. The price of our land is not yet above its earning value, but the protectionists' of this country want to protect us as the United States farmer is protected on the other side of the line, where somebody else gets the land and the farmer has to go away on foot. When the price of land gets above its earning power and will not pay interest on the investment, no matter what protection you may have, if. you have to depend on the export market, you are not going to be able to protect that farmer. But the United States farmer is in a little different position to-day. He does not get as good a price for the produce he exports at the present time as for that part of his produce which is used at home in case of a few articles and they of course are human. After the bad condition they got into, the politician came along who wanted to make political capital out of the bad condition of the farmers. The position was much the same as that brought by the St. Lawrence and great waterways agitation. They are putting words in the mouths of the people of the West and making them say they want the great waterways. That is what the politicians did to the farmers in the United States who had lost their homes and were unable to pay their way out of the produce they were raising on those farms. I spent five weeks in the United States last summer, and I can tell hon. members that the



The Budget-Mr. Warner
farmers there are beginning to see that they are not getting the benefit out of the tariff that my hon. friend thinks they are. They tell me they have had absolutely no benefit from the Fordney tariff at the present time, and it has been the politicians in the United States who asked for the tariff, rather than the farmers themselves. The same thing is going on in Canada to-day. In my opinion it is absolutely dangerous to make political capital out of either tariff protection or free trade. I have never in my lifetime known any subject which has befuddled, mixed, and that bothered the people as much as the tariff has. It is a complicated affair, and people who are not willing to take a great deal of pains and make a study of it could be made to believe it could do anything, and that is what has happened in Canada. [DOT] I think the time has come in Canada, before we get into a worse condition than we are in at the present time, that people should have some consideration for what is good for the country, rather than for what is good to build up a political party.
Western development as we have had it is a matter that is fresh in my mind. I understand it a little better than the building up and development that went on in the United States, so many years ago, although that is quite plain to me. I left there some twenty-five years ago, and I have been more or less out of touch with conditions. But I feel that I am understanding western conditions and what has happened out West. When I first went into that country we could get land very cheaply. The first land I bought was near the little town of Ed-montort; it cost me a little less than $6 an acre, and I bought quite a good sized farm. On that investment in the land we could earn a good return, and things looked bright to me. My boys were growing up on the farm, and we made money under those conditions. By and by the boom came on and people began to throw money into that country for investment, and to buy land for speculation. They bought land to sell again, and not for what they could make out of it by farming. That spirit ran away with the people for a while. The same thing happened in the United States. They boomed the land, and of course the land rose in price. We have stopped short of the calamity which has befallen the farmers of the United States, as far as the price of land is concerned. We can make something out of our land here. If a man buys land in western Canada judiciously, it is possible in ordinary times to earn an income on the money he puts into it. Farming was not so attractive to people for 
a few years. They wanted to buy a farm and sell it again. They would buy it for an investment, allow it to remain there and increase in value. They purchased the land for the sake of the increased value rather than for what they could get out of the land by way of production. That went on for some time, but it has stopped now, just as it has in the United States. At different periods the same thing happened to the United States that is now happening in western Canada. We are in a condition now in western Canada where we must farm and dig out of the soil what we make, because the money is not coming into that country for future returns on investment or for speculation as it was a few years ago.
It is very difficult for the farmers out in the West now to make any sort of living. It is now that the people are beginning to feel the depression, just as they did in the United States at certain times in the history of those people; and reductions in the tariff are now most welcome. It is simply because the farmers of western Canada have suffered from this depression that they have sent their representatives here to tell parliament that they absolutely cannot stand it any longer. They are unable to dig money out of the ground fast enough to pay for their farms, and to meet their other obligations. So we think that the government has taken a step in the right direction in beginning to reduce the tariff, and we ask that everything possible be done as well in every other way to provide some relief for the people. There are many things that need to be done; one thing alone will not suffice. When money flooded the country we did not feel any depression and the tariff did not appear to the people then as a very great burden; but to-day, labouring under the depressing influence of conditions as they exist in this country, if the people are to be saved, their burdens must be lightened. I repeat, the tariff alone will not do everything; but it certainly will help to a considerable extent, and while I may not live to see free trade adopted in Canada I do hope that I shall live to see the time when we shall at least have a tariff for revenue rather than for protection and just as near free trade as is possible or practical. I know from my experience in the United States that in that country the people were visited with periods of depression just as we are suffering to-day; these times of depression come and they go. But so far as Canada is concerned, I am afraid that if something is not done there may come a time when the depression will come to stay. I do not want

The Budget-Mr. [Varner
to be considered a calamity howler for a moment because I believe that it is possible for the country to get fairly well on its feet if the government will do all that it can. And we have the promise that they will do more next year, or at any rate at some time in the future, than they have done in the present budget in the way of reducing the cost of living. We also need lower transportation rates, so that the people may get their products to market with the least possible delay and at the lowest cost. These are the problems which we must solve. I know something about manufacturing, because, I may remark, farming is not my only interest. I am connected with manufacturing industries and I know that we must borrow money; and when money is borrowed the concern must pay interest on it first of all before it can make a profit. What happens? That interest is charged in the price of the article we produce or taken off the price of the raw material. And there is no other way out of the difficulty; the business cannot be run otherwise. I am just ps satisfied as I am that I am standing here to-night that Canada to-day is paying too much for the . use of money which she has to procure to do business with. It is not only desirable but it will be absolutely necessary to reduce the rate of interest, and if the bankers and other money lenders are determined to maintain a high rate they will meet disaster without a doubt. They have no right to hold up the people and make them pay more than they can possibly afford for the use of money. At present this seems unavoidable. There has been a lot of talk about the banking system, and I believe that conditions in western Canada would have been better if it had not been. so easy for people to borrow money. The bankers induced them to borrow when things were in a flourishing state and the time is not opportune now to force people to pay high rates of interest on their obligations. If the interest that a country has to pay on the money it requires is higher than it can stand, surely it is in the best interests of national economy that the rate should be reduced, but the individual person or company can not do this alone, it will have to come through a concerted action; it seems to me that it would be better for the money lenders to charge a reasonable interest which people can afford to pay than to demand a high rate of interest which it is impossible for ordinary people to put up. The manager of one loaning company in the West with whom I am acquainted informs me that by reason of the judicious placing of his money he has 107j
not lost one cent during the past few years. I cannot remember whether he said it was within the past five or seven years, but I am inclined to think that it was since the war that he said he had suffered no losses, having disposed of his money judiciously, of course. The people to whom he would lend money were those who could afford to pay, while those who could not pay had to go to the wall. Everybody, of course, expects security for money that is borrowed, and it is better that way. But if the interest is 8 per cent and the people cannot afford more than 4 per cent, would it not be better for the lenders to take 4 per cent, even though they might suffer some hardship along with other people until things became normal again?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman fix the rate of interest by statute?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not know about
that. My hon. friend is a lawyer and he knows more about these things.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I deny the soft impeachment.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
You have to draw the
line somewhere.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am not going to say where we should draw the line but I do say that it would be better for the lenders to take a reasonable rate of interest rather than ask for an exorbitant amount. When I was a young man I was not blessed with much money; I was pretty much in the same position as my hon. friend who spoke a little while ago (Mr. Spence). I often had to borrow money from the banks and I know how difficult it was to meet their conditions. In the state of Nebraska where I lived-and bankers are pretty much alike all the world over-there was a legal rate of interest of 7 per cent, and on special contracts 10 per cent per annum. The remarkable thing was that when a man borrowed money the banker deducted from the sum he gave him an amount covering the first year's interest. I can tell hon. gentlemen that it was not a very pleasant experience for me, for I have paid all the way from 10 per cent to 24 per cent; I have been asked as high as 36 per cent, but I never paid more than 24 per cent, although the bankers were operating under a law of the state of Nebraska that entitled them to 7 per cent interest when rate not specified but with an interest of 10 per cent on special contracts. They circumvented the law, and I do not know that the bankers here would not do the same. I am not saying that they would; I do not know whether they would or not. I do not
The Budget-Mr. Werner

know whether we can regulate the rate of interest by statute, but, if possible, it seems to me it would be good business to do so, for if the money is not worth what our people are being charged for it the bankers themselves will suffer because after a while they are going to be like the darkey-they will be trying to do business when there is no business available.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If parliament were to fix
the rate of interest chargeable by banks at a moderate figure, would it not tend to drive the poor borrower into the hands of the rapacious money-lender, who charges ten, twelve or fourteen per cent interest?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That might be so, but
I would tell my hon. friend this:	I do not
believe that the poor borrower is in very merciful or tender hands at the present time.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I quite agree.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
So, after a man is broke
I do not think it makes much difference where he goes for accommodation; he is bound to have a hard time anyway. I am not asking that money be loaned to anybody who cannot give security. It is unfortunate, but the human family is built that way: we do not want to put our money out at interest where we see little prospect of ever getting it back. But it is my opinion that our civilization cannot stand the rate of interest which is being charged to-day, and I fear that if the people are forced to the wall one at a time it will eventually lead to their rising as a body and exacting penalties.
I did not expect to get into this line of argument, in fact I drifted into it. But I think it is important to say this: I believe that restricted purchasing power is a part of our trouble. I do not believe that the tariff is to blame for all of our troubles, or anywhere near all. It was said by my leader (Mr. Forke) this afternoon that it is not worth while for the manufacturing interests or the protectionists to undertake to raise the price of their goods by raising the tariff. That that is not the way out is my honest, sincere conviction. I do not think that the manufacturer can help himself out of his troubles by raising the price of his product. I believe that to-day our manufacturers are suffering simply because the people are not able to buy the manufactured goods that are being turned out. It is this inability on the part of the people to buy, this lack of purchasing power, which is hurting the manufacturers to a far greater extent than outside competition. For example, in my own part of the country the people are fixing

up their old machines. These old machines are not really capable of doing good work, but their owners are disinclined to pay the price for new machinery. Well, if the price is already too high, how are the manufacturers of such machinery going to increase their sales if they advance their prices? I told the House a little while ago that I was connected with a couple of important business concerns. Our experience there is that the most satisfactory results are obtained by increasing our turnover at low prices rather than by securing higher prices on a small turnover.
Although I presume that some may think it not good taste on my part to offer advice to our manufacturers, still, I think I know a little about how to carry on business, and therefore I tell them that many of them would be better off if they would mark down the selling price of their products, reduce their manufacturing cost, squeeze the water out of their capital stock, and get down to a real valuation of their actual operating capital. I do not care how much money I might make on the transaction, no man could sell me watered stock. I have had lots of opportunities to buy watered stock in various companies, but I am not out to make money in this way. I do not know how many of our manufacturing concerns have watered stock, but certainly I am not in favour of such concerns attempting to get a return on watered stock by means of charging high prices on a lessened turnover, which would be the result of their securing higher protection.
There is just a question in my mind whether my advice in this respect would be absolutely sound. I admit this, because it is my opinion that our farm implement manufacturers already have the power and ability to turn out more implements than Canada would be able to buy, even at lower prices. To meet the situation these manufacturers must be willing to do as we farmers have done; when we raise more wheat than we can sell for domestic consumption we sell it in the world's market and take what we can get for it, and the price we obtain fixes the domestic price. I am well aware that our manufacturers would hold up their hands in holy horror at such a suggestion. They say that they cannot do this. But they are already doing it. They are exporting their implements and selling them for less than we can buy them for in Canada. We have the price of our wheat at home set largely by the surplus that we export. If the manufacturers would take their medicine

and do likewise they would bring money back into Canada and so help business, which would be a great deal better than their trying to make Canadians pay more lor what the manufacturers offer for sale. I do not see how our manufacturers would really be benefited if they could raise the price of their product by protection. I do not believe that we farmers could afford to put a price on our wheat and say thalt we would not sell until we got that price; we could not do it. But I do know that the whole Dominion is dependent very largely on the output of the farm, and that agricultural prosperity is at once reflected in every other channel of business. The money that comes in from our produce sold outside is new money in this country, and we are that much better off each year. Although the farmer may lose money on his personal operations, Canada alt. large has that much more wealth at home.
The home market is all right, and I want to see more of it. But my hair is too grey to wait till the 'home market can take care of the extra produce that I want to raise on my farms. I have a note here: Why are our people leaving Canada to go to the United States? There has been a good deal of discussion about this question. I do not claim to be sufficiently well posted to know just how many of our people have migrated to the United States to make their homes there, and I doubt whether anyone else knows either. But there muslt be something in what everybody talks about. I do not know that I can tell in every case just why our people are going to the United States in such numbers.
It makes me feel that some hon. members are playing politics when they talk about people leaving the country on account of the present budget, though it has not yet gone through the House. It seems to me that is a little previous, a little premature. I believe that more people have gone to the United States on account of protection than ever thought of going on account of this budget. Some of the best people I ever lived amongst came from Canada into the neighbourhood where I was, and settled there, and I grew up among them. I liked the Canadians, and I like them now; they have always treated me well. But why were these people going over there thirty or forty years ago? They did not go on account of this budget, that is sure; but they have been going right along, although we have had protection for forty years. Hon. gentlemen cannot afford to make political capital out of the present condition of this country. If we would come here with the best
The Budget-Mr. Warner
interests of our country at heart, thinking nothing 'of politics, nothing of strengthening our party or of whether or not the people would send us back here; if we would simply get down to business and think of the welfare of the country instead of the interests of the party we belong to, we would make more progress. Canada is a big country; it is a rich country and we could have more people; but if we want people to come here we should not be squabbling among ourselves about what keeps them away. We have great natural resources and we should bend our energies to bringing enough people here to secure their development. But when we bring people here we must do everything that is possible to make them prosperous.
It is a fallacy to say that the United States has been made prosperous by its protective tariff; rather it should be said that the United States has been made prosperous in spite of its protective tariff. I say this after living in that country until I was middle-aged, and I know something about it. You will bring Canada to the position you desire much quicker by lowering the tariff so that living will be cheaper and conditions will be more attractive in all lines of activity. And let everybody make up his mind to earn what he gets rather than to make a profit on speculations, increased land values, watered stocks, and so on. The immigrants who come here come, for the most part, to a better country than they left, and the chances of their being prosperous are likely to be much better here than they were in their native land. We could have three or four times the number of people that we now have and still be prosperous, and it would be easier to solve the problems which face us. We want to make living on the land attractive so that the people will make their homes there and stay there; we want to have it so that the people would rather live on the land than anywhere else. I do not know how much it is possible for this government to do, but I believe that the lowering of the tariff would help along that line.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Would the hon.
gentleman favour the lowering of the tariff on agricultural products?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Well, the question is all right, and I am glad to have it. I do not know what the hon. member refers to. I do not believe I raise anything that has benefited by the tariff that is on it now.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How about butter?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The tariff on butter is only four cents.
The Budget-Mr. Warner

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is it enough?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am not asking for a higher tariff on butter. I am not saying anything about the tariff on butter. But there is a duty of 8 cents on our butter going to the United States, and I would rather see them take off 4 cents over there and bring it down to what ours is.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But they will not do it. What about the tariff on meat?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not want to get into a discussion on the tariff on meat. But it is not possible to help the farmers of this country by a tariff on butter or meat or anything of that kind, because we are going to raise more and more of those products and send them out to the world market. That will make the price on the home market rather than the tariff having anything to do with it.
With regard to the amendment, I would like to have an opportunity to support some of the items mentioned in it, although I think it will frighten our protectionist friends and those who are asking for protection on both sides of the House. I do not know that there are any of those in this group to the left; it is the only group that does not have protection in mind.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There are one or two of them there.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not know about them. Now, I am not standing here and boasting of what I have, but I am not a pauper, and I want to say that I am absolutely in favour of increasing the income tax and using any money we have over to pay off our national debt. Where a man has an income of fair amount we know that there is a source of revenue, but if we impose large taxes on the smaller income of the man who has a family we are making it hard for them to get along. It is difficult to get money for business purposes when you have a very high income tax, but if those who have money in this country are patriotic they will put it into manufacturing enterprises and thus help the country to go ahead, rather than hide it away in their stocking. So I say .we should get the money where it can be got, and we should increase the income tax. I do not say that I want to see the income tax continually increased from time to time indefinitely, but we have a debt in this country that we have to pay, and we have to dig it out of this country. The money is not going to be sent in here to pay it. If you take the money from the man who is able to pay. it will help pay our debt. I do not see how you 
are going to pay it unless you take it where it can be got.
There is another tax I would like to heartily support, and that is the inheritance tax. The question is raised whether the Dominion or the provincial governments should impose such a tax, but no matter in which field it lies, I think it would be a good wav of raising money. If a man has raised a family in Canada and they are not able to take care of themselves, but are dependent on what money he has made during his lifetime, they are rather a handicap than a benefit to Canada. I am a little doubtful whether anyone who is not willing to work for a living and make his own way, and' who lives on the money left by large estates, is not rather a detriment to the country. So I say we should take quite a lot of money from the large estates, and let the children do what the parents did, earn their own living and become good citizens. They will develop themselves much better in that way than if they are allowed to spend inherited money in riotous living. Whether the provincial governments or the federal government impose the tax makes no difference in principle.
Coming now to the amendment and the proposed reduction on clothing and the necessaries of life, there is not much of a tariff on food stuffs of such kinds as we produce in Canada at the present time. So far as clothing is concerned, I suppose that the man who produced the wool in this suit I am wearing would not get much more than two dollars for it. I had the figures, but I have not them with me now, and I am doing a little guessing. This suit cost me with two pairs of trousers $75. That is too much protection for me. The same prevails in many other lines particularly in boots and shoes.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Wool is on the free list.	[DOT]

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is one on me, if
it is, but I have had scores of petitions and blotters coming to me saying, "Don't blot out this industry; give us protection." So if they have not protection now, they must be asking for it.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Woollens are not on the free list, but the raw wool is.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I know what the hon
member says is true. I have the patriotism of the manufacturer right down in my head real good. An hon. member to my right during his speech was asked why the manufacturer did not use the native raw material, and he replied that the manufacturer could buy cheaper material from the other side

The Budget-Mr. Warner
and get just as much for it when he sold his product, or pretty nearly so. Now that is patriotism with a vengeance.
If the manufacturer would stand right up to his work, and turn out his goods as cheap as he could, if he would do as the farmers are doing in this country, we should be a double team then and we could make this country go; but as it is now the manufacturer-and I know because I am in the business of manufacturing myself-passes along all the expenses of his business to the consumer to pay, or takes it out of the producer of the raw material. He wants the other fellow shut out of the country so that he will not have to sell in competition with him, and he wants to put the people out of business, like the nigger that wanted to keep store after the people'were dead. That is how patriotic they are, in my opinion.
As to the manufacturer of farm implements, there are millions of dollars worth of farm implements piled up in factories and storehouses in this country, lying on the hands of the manufacturers, which would not be there if we had not had protection to the manufacturer for the last forty years. The manufacturer is reaping the result of that policy now, because the people are not able to buy what he has to sell, and he, has to quit business. He has blocked his own game.
I am ready for questions on that. He has blocked his own game, and now he wants protection in order to accomplish an impossibility. He wants to try and lift himself by his boot straps.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Is that the
reason Why the farmer is importing some $13,000,000 odd of agricultural implements as againsit a local sale of some $18,000,000? He can afford to buy the imported article.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I will admit frankly I do not know just what implements are being imported and sold. They may be selling them, but I do not know anybody who is buying many of them. If the manufacturer were as patriotic as I think he ought to be, he would pay an excise duty equal to the duty paid on these implements entering Canada, because he can make them as cheaply as the manufacturer he is competing with. And whenever the manufacturer is ready to pay that excise duty, I am willing to give him protection, because we have to raise the revenue to run the country.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Would the hon. member
also include an excise duty of 4 cents a pound on butter?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Absolutely, if it ever
amounts to that much protection to our business. As far as I am concerned I can promise that. I am manufacturing butter, and I know who pays the bill. The man who produces the cream is the man that pays the bill. I am a farmer and cream producer as well as a manufacturer of butter and I would be the goat for myself as well as for all the rest of the Canadian manufacturers. We have to pay interest and overhead, and he would have to take the loss. I do not want to see that, although it would not hurt our concern personally and it would not hurt the other manufacturer to stand it either, because he passes it on to the buyer.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Would it hurt the
farmer?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It would hurt the farmer, he would have to take that much less for his cream. And it has to be that way; a business has got to pay its overhead or it cannot keep running. We cannot pass on that duty in the price of butter, for that price is fixed in the world market.
Now, I was talking about the amendment.
I have said that I would like to get an opportunity to vote for some of the things in that amendment but when they are coupled with other questions I do not see how I can do so. Talk about your natural resources! We are going to have our premier down here from Alberta in a few days asking for these natural resources. Now, we do not want the Dominion government to levy taxes on these resources if we get them. We want those resources for what there is in them; and if the Dominion government cannot levy, as proposed by the amendment, on those resources, then they are going to be short the amount of money that taxation would represent. I do not know how they are going to calculate the amount. I could not do it offhand, I should have to study the question out and it would take some time before the system would be running properly anyway. But I want to see the province tax its natural resources. We are already paying on land values, and as to this question there is a whole lot of myth. There is a lot of talk by people who do not own land. I own land myself and I know something about the question. We are paying about all we can pay for land at the present time, but that is not my objection to this proposition. I repeat that land value is a myth. I want to tell you this:	I have been
a good deal of my time where land was not
The Budget-Mr. Warner

worth .a cent an acre. Go out into a new country where there is absolutely nothing done. That is the only way that you can put a price on unimproved land values. It has been done otherwise, 'but it is largely guess work. Some of my land near Edmonton is valued for taxing purposes at $50 per acre. Land farther back is valued at less, considerably less; but it all depends on the improvements in Edmonton. I say again land value is a myth, you do not know what you are going to get when you put a tax on land values. I have worked for a tax on unimproved land values, but since I have been studying the question I have been wondering how much there is in it-I really have.
Now, when I consider the items in the amendment I do not think that I can support it conscientiously, although I should like to get some of the things that are mentioned in it. There is another point. We have a government in Canada and hon. gentlemen opposite are running it for us.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: With you.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am not ready to vote a want of confidence in the government at the present time.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That sounds reasonable.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That brings a smile to the face of the Acting Finance Minister.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am absolutely conscientious when I say this.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Could you not do better?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I feel that it would be no benefit to us to defeat the government at the present time. We have their promise that they are going to lower the tariff to a greater extent than any other government has done in Canada.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: This is along the line that I would like to see action taken.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Lower the duty on what?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not care to discuss that question now offhand. I think the hon. gentleman knows better than I do just what is involved. I repeat that I am not ready to give a vote of want of confidence in the government just for the sake of putting them out. Of course it will not be done; I know that amendment cannot carry, still if I am honest and vote according to my conscience, as I try to do, I would want that to carry; but if I voted for it that would mean that I 
wish the government to be put out of business, if I understand it rightly. Now, I am not ready to put them out of business, because I want to hold them to their promises in tariff reductions with a chance to see results. That is the p.oint-we want results, results in the form of legislation that will give greater freedom for development to the basic industries of this country, and we will join our efforts with those of any other hon. members of this House who are ready to work with us on that line.
On motion of Mr. LeSueur, the debate was adjourned.
On motion of Mr. Graham, the House adjourned at 10.59 p.m.
